entries.title: Bears report: Offensive line uncertainty as Jonah Jackson injured, decision to make at left tackle
entries.summary: <p>What happened Monday at Halas Hall:</p><h3><b>Jackson in jeopardy</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> didn’t practice Monday, but were required to release an estimated injury report and didn’t think right guard Jonah Jackson (hip) would’ve been available. Jackson went down in the second half of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/18/bears-cb-kyler-gordon-goes-off-with-3-sacks-in-return-from-injury-everything-i-wanted" >the win over the Falcons</a>, and Luke Newman replaced him. Jackson hasn’t missed a start in two seasons with the Bears.</p><p></p><h3><b>Monangai still sidelined</b></h3><h3></h3><p>No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai, an integral part of the ground game alongside D’Andre Swift, looks unlikely to be back against the Patriots. Monangai has missed two games with a toe injury, and the Bears said he wouldn’t have practiced Monday. If he’s out, Roschon Johnson is likely to continue getting a decent share of carries.</p><p></p><h3><b>Doubs out</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Patriots put wide receiver Romeo Doubs, formerly of the Packers, on injured reserve with a shoulder injury. He leads them with 261 yards and three touchdowns.</p><p></p><h3><b>Bagent stays backup</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Tyson Bagent’s spot as the backup quarterback was in question after he got benched against the Packers, but coach Ben Johnson kept him in the No. 2 spot Sunday and made third-stringer Case Keenum the inactive emergency quarterback.</p><p></p><h3><b>Left tackle decision</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Bears eventually want Ozzy Trapilo to step back into his spot as the starting left tackle, and playing a few series Sunday in his season debut was a step toward that. Ben Johnson must weigh whether he’s ready for more or to stay predominantly with Theo Benedet.</p>

entries.title: Gabby Williams is just another former Sky player to flourish elsewhere
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — If only the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> had had a clearer vision for Gabby Williams.</p><p>When they drafted her out of UConn with the No. 4 overall pick in 2018, they weren’t exactly sure how to use her. Sometimes she played the four, sometimes the three. Sometimes she was a backup point guard, despite never having played the position before.</p><p>She told retired WNBA star Sue Bird on her podcast last year that, in those years, she felt like “the duct tape that closes the leaks.”</p><p>Now that she’s the engine of the Valkyries, her services are more than just leak closure. The offense relies desperately on her ability to scamper around and make jump shots. The defense feeds off her athleticism.</p><p>That led to a big problem Monday night during Game 2 of the WNBA Finals: Shots weren’t falling for Williams, who had four steals but finished with 14 points on 3-for-15 shooting. The Valkyries didn’t quite know where else to turn, eventually falling 79-65 to the Dream to even the best-of-seven series at one game apiece.</p><p>It was quite the opposite story for former Sky forward Angel Reese, who poured in 30 points and pulled down 16 rebounds for the Dream after struggling down the stretch in the series opener Saturday.</p><p>“For me, I think I let my team down last game, not really contributing as much as I could in the second half,” said Reese, who became the third player in WNBA history with at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a Finals game, joining Jonquel Jones for the Sun in 2019 and Breanna Stewart for the Storm in 2020. “I just wanted to make sure I came out tonight and left my mark and did whatever I could to get the win, and I think I did that.”</p><p>Rhyne Howard set a Finals record with six steals, and fellow guard Allisha Gray added 18 points as the Dream won a Finals game for the first time after going 0-10 in their previous three trips.</p><p>The Valkyries will try to get the advantage back Wednesday in Atlanta, hoping for a stronger night from Williams, whose path to stardom has been unique because her confidence blossomed outside the WNBA. Playing overseas helped her find a role as a wing scorer and showed she could be a centerpiece, not just a complement.</p><p>She also was paid much better. Maximum contracts in the WNBA used to be capped at $250,000; elite players could earn far more internationally. As negotiations on a collective-bargaining agreement dragged on in 2025, most of the game’s biggest stars claimed the WNBA wasn’t paying them what they were worth. Williams had argued that for years.</p><p>Having been raised in part by her grandmother, who is French, Williams also prioritized her commitment to the French national team, helping to turn it into a powerhouse that almost beat Team USA in the 2026 FIBA World Cup championships and the 2024 Olympic gold-medal game. After the latter, Reese, then a Sky rookie, jokingly tweeted that Williams should come play for the Sky. But by that time, she’d had enough of Chicago. Not only was she discouraged by her limited role during her Sky days, but management hadn’t exactly given her a positive impression about its willingness to invest in the player experience.</p><p>There also had been miscommunication with the Sky’s front office surrounding Williams’ commitment to the French national team in 2021. Williams thought she’d reached an agreement with the Sky that she didn’t have to show up to training camp. Then, when she didn’t, the Sky suspended her contract and traded her to the Sparks.</p><p>“I think I was always like, ‘[The team] is my family,’ ” she said on Bird’s podcast. “Like, I eat lunch with them. You know, [former Sky general manager and coach James Wade’s] wife was French. We were hanging out all the time. [But] I was like, ‘These people are not your friends, Gabby. They’re not your family.’</p><p>“It forced me to change the way I think about these things and make better decisions for myself versus sacrificing my well-being, which I was doing before, to just be anything for the team. I was like, ‘You know what? I’m going to be selfish. Like, I’m going to make decisions for me now.’ ”</p><p>Her latest decision proved to be a good one. She signed a maximum contract worth $1.19 million with the Valkyries, a team that looks set up for success for years to come.</p><p>Contributing: AP</p>

entries.title: Gas in Chicago is now more than $5 a gallon. Does buying a hybrid make sense?
entries.summary: <h3>What are hybrid vehicles?</h3><p>Hybrid vehicles have been in the U.S. market for more than two decades. A hybrid has a gas engine, a small battery and an electric motor. Hybrids don’t need to be plugged in, unlike electric vehicles. A hybrid’s electric motor drives the car at low speeds, and a gas engine runs at higher speeds or recharging the battery, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/hybrids-evs/why-hybrid-vehicles-are-a-smart-choice-right-now-a2736240282/?EXTKEY=SG72C02&gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=13041205141&gbraid=0AAAAAD-SwFTEUcx0qwWNvJ4YXNY47I2VD&gclid=CjwKCAjwoaLWBhAWEiwAnyituymXOm03ey0sI4JNzyLX2jtfkVTxfY_NU6NptZiyki90At18EdOr9xoCsrkQAvD_BwE" target="_blank" ><u>Consumer Reports</u></a>. </p><p>They can be good options for longer trips or for areas without charging stations. The Toyota Prius, which gets 49 to 57 miles per gallon depending on model, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.kbb.com/car-advice/prius-mpg-solid-choice-hybrid/" target="_blank" ><u>Kelley Blue Book,</u></a> is an example of a hybrid.</p><p>There are also <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/hybrids-evs/how-to-decide-if-a-hybrid-plug-in-hybrid-or-fully-electric-c-a6216376327/" target="_blank" ><u>plug-in hybrids</u></a> for driving locally on electric and on gas for longer distances.</p><h3>Have sales of hybrids and electric vehicles increased?</h3><p>Sales of hybrids increased to a record 16% of all U.S. car sales by the second quarter this year, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67885" target="_blank" ><u>Energy Information Administration</u></a>. The growth of hybrids is an example of pressure on household budgets and a focus on affordability influencing consumers, said <a class="Link" href="https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights/affordability-challenges-reshape-automotive-demand/" target="_blank" ><u>Cox Automotive</u></a>.</p><p>Last year, electric vehicle sales spiked ahead of the end of federal tax credits in September 2025 under President Donald Trump’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12625?__cf_chl_tk=me39dlOaCEcY65G_3K8ojlWURF8qFwY.hqDd_SbQ4kyw-1790882359-1.0.1.1-7HChWDax9ZlA33_f3KUDjSl9tPk3Rdy51txgi8txqY4" target="_blank" ><u>One Big Beautiful Bill Act</u></a>. As expected, EV sales fell after tax credits were eliminated. </p><p>This year, EVs accounted for 6.5% of U.S. car sales in the third quarter, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights/q3-2026-ev-sales-report-commentary/" target="_blank" ><u>Cox Automotive</u></a>. Nearly 25% of all vehicle sales in the third quarter were electric vehicles, including hybrid EVs and plug-in models. In Cook County, there were more than 124,000 hybrids as of August, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilsos.gov/content/dam/departments/vehicles/statistics/hybrid/2026/hybrid081526.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois data</u></a>.</p><h3>Do hybrids save money on gas?</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.kbb.com/car-advice/hybrid-evs/" target="_blank" ><u>Hybrids</u></a><u> </u>are typically more expensive than conventional counterparts. For example, the 2026 Toyota Corolla LE costs $24,595, while the 2026 Corolla Hybrid LE costs $25,970, said<a class="Link" href="https://www.kbb.com/car-advice/hybrid-vs-gas-break-even-fuel-savings/" target="_blank" > <u>Kelley Blue Book</u></a>. But the hybrid model returns 50 miles per gallon combined compared to 34 miles per gallon for the gas-powered vehicle. With<a class="Link" href="https://gasprices.aaa.com/?state=IL" target="_blank" > <u>gas prices</u></a> in Chicago at $5.05 per gallon as of Monday, the conventional car has an annual fuel cost of $2,232 when driving 15,000 miles per year, according to Kelley Blue Book’s<a class="Link" href="https://www.kbb.com/car-advice/hybrid-vs-gas-break-even-fuel-savings/" target="_blank" > <u>hybrid fuel savings calculator</u></a>. A hybrid would cost $1,518 per year to fuel, amounting to $714 in annual savings compared to the gas-powered car. It would take one year and 11 months to recoup the higher cost of the hybrid.</p><h3>When does driving a hybrid make sense?</h3><p>Hybrids are better for driving around the city. The electric motors of hybrids do more of the work at low speeds and in stop-and-go traffic, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.kbb.com/car-advice/hybrid-vs-gas-break-even-fuel-savings/" target="_blank" ><u>Kelley Blue Book</u></a>. But for highway driving and long distances, hybrids rely on the gas engine, which reduces fuel savings.</p><h3>What else should I know? </h3><p>Hybrid systems can reduce maintenance on brake pads, the gas engine and some traditional parts, such as alternators, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.edmunds.com/car-buying/hybrid-vehicle-pros-cons.html" target="_blank" ><u>Edmunds</u></a>. But replacing a hybrid’s battery pack after about a decade can cost thousands of dollars.</p><p>Some hybrid owners report more difficulty finding mechanics for repairs and maintenance. Edmunds lists other pros and cons, including the environmental benefits of burning less gasoline. Ultimately, whether a hybrid is worth the investment comes down to its initial sticker price, gas mileage, fuel prices, yearly driving distance, and how long you plan to own it.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Grandpa lives closer but still keeps to himself
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My parents divorced when I was 5 years old, and my father moved out of state shortly afterward. For many years, I rarely saw him in person. However, he stayed in touch through phone calls and letters, and he always called on my birthday and holidays. Eventually, he settled in Alaska, far from where I lived. Even with the distance, he remained a consistent presence by phone in my life.</p><p>He recently retired and now lives about an hour and a half away from me. I'm a father myself now, and I want him to be a part of both my life and my children's lives while he has time left. The problem is that he's a hermit who seems content to stay at home. Over the years, he has missed many important moments in my life, like my wedding, my college graduation and most of my children's milestones.</p><p>My youngest son graduates this month, and although I've invited my father, he says he has other plans. I have even offered to pick him up and take him home if driving is difficult. I know he loves his grandkids; he texts them and tells them he's proud of them. I can't force him to be more involved, and I'm beginning to wonder whether I should stop trying. What advice do you have? — <i>MISSING DAD</i></p><p><b>DEAR MISSING:</b> Unless your dad seems bothered by your attempts to include him, continue inviting him to every event. He may not attend, but his texts indicate that he's interested in his grandkids' lives.</p><p>It can be hard for older people to get around, and he may feel it would be too burdensome to let you play chauffeur. You didn't mention any health problems, but 90 minutes in a car is more than even some healthy seniors would want to consider. Why not make time to take your kids to his town for a visit? I'm not suggesting you invade his home, but an announced day trip to get him out of the house might be good for everyone.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My spouse passed away from pancreatic cancer more than two years ago. We were together for 13 years and stood by each other during good and bad times. I was recently contacted by my first love from 44 years ago. We've been emailing, and I've been feeling emotions about him like when we were younger. My heart beats faster when he writes, yet I feel guilty because I was prepared never to care for anyone again. Is it possible to find someone to love me in my early 60s? Part of me feels scared to make a fool of myself, so it's confusing. — <i>FUTURE LOVE IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR FUTURE LOVE:</b> Yes, it is indeed possible. The emotions you're feeling are proof that you're alive. Folks in their 60s and beyond have been known to find love again. You may be one of the lucky ones. The important thing is to let this relationship play out in its own time and not try to rush it.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: ‘Chicago Music, Seen: 100 Portraits’ chronicles 50 years of the city’s evolving, diverse music scenes
entries.summary: <p>Pics or it didn’t happen. That’s the takeaway after scrolling through the collection of photos in the new coffee table book “Chicago Music, Seen.”</p><p>Across 200 pages, music photographer and Evanston native Jim Newberry corrals his most candid snapshots and telling portraits of local luminaries like Liz Phair, Tortoise, Buddy Guy and Andrew Bird to present a visual trip through Chicago’s evolving and diverse music scenes over the last five decades, from blues and rock to hip-hop and house music.</p><p>“At the time, I was just kind of shooting assignments. But looking back on it from the macro view, it's interesting to see the different scenes and how they evolved,” said the photographer, now based in L.A. </p><p>Laid out chronologically, “Chicago Music, Seen” (out Oct. 20 on University of Illinois Press) features an impressive amount of Newberry’s work from 1987 to 2023, the same images that frequently appeared in the Chicago Reader<i> </i>or as promos or album artwork for local labels like Touch and Go, Thrill Jockey and DJ International Records. Each page also features commentary from journalists or stories from the subjects themselves, resetting the scene and significance of the moment captured.</p><p> Newberry’s initial inspiration for the craft came from father, James Newberry (no relation to the library) who started the photography department at Columbia College in 1967. </p><p>“He got me interested at a young age. I started shooting probably when I was 9 or 10,” Jim said. </p><p>Years later, Newberry’s high school friend Kriss Bataille was his gateway into documenting the city’s music scene. Bataille was the short-lived drummer in Urge Overkill, and when the band needed images for their “Lineman” single in the late ’80s, Newberry was recommended. That resulting photo is one of the earliest in the book; the final entry captures a new era of Girls of the Golden West in 2023.</p><p>From that pivotal first assignment, you could find Newberry hanging out at his favorite music clubs Lounge Ax and the Hideout, working from his loft studio in Pilsen or invited into the homes of legends like Mavis Staples to get the perfect shot. While he had thousands of images to choose from, Newberry narrowed it down to the best 100. </p><p>“My main criteria was pictures that I thought were good photos, regardless of how famous or talented the artist was,” he said.</p><p>Below, Newberry shares the behind-the-scenes details from some of his favorites. You can hear more when Newberry appears Saurday at the Museum of Post Punk & Industrial Music, 3319 S. Lituanica Ave. Find tickets at <a class="Link" href="http://ppimchicago.com" target="_blank" ><u>ppimchicago.com</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Photos: Chicago Fashion Week show is first to celebrate work from all openly LGBTQ+ designers
entries.summary: <p>Each year, <a class="Link" href="https://chicagofashionweek.com/" target="_blank" >Chicago Fashion Week</a> stages creations by local designers through a series of events and runway shows.</p><p>But this year brought a first: More than a hundred attendees gathered at an art gallery in Chicago’s Wicker Park neighborhood last Thursday for the sold-out <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/queercouturerunway/" target="_blank" ><u>Queer Couture Runway</u></a> show. Executive producer Madison Smith and artistic director Emry Yarger said it was the first event in Chicago Fashion Week to explicitly state it was created by queer creatives to highlight queerness in design.</p><p>The show featured <a class="Link" href="https://www.canva.com/design/DAHXh8xcZgM/2Cz7y0UWHosiefLRd5ey3g/view?utm_content=DAHXh8xcZgM&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link&utm_source=viewer" target="_blank" ><u>nine designers</u></a> ranging in experience levels and styles. Organizers said the idea for centering the show around queerness came up organically.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure They wanted to create an environment of openness for up-and-coming designers looking to try new ideas.</p><p>“Black and Brown, queer and trans people set our culture across the board, and that deserves to be honored and recognized,” said Yarger. “I am super hopeful that this was a space for folks with those identities, for all queer folks, to present their work and to show how they are the tastemakers of our whole culture.”</p><p>The list of designers included In Between Branches, Daisy In Chains and Jaluda by Antonio Arcé. For some designers, it was their first time creating a collection. Gregory Pagán-Hill, who goes by the moniker Uncle Greg, said he’s been sewing since he was a child. His work is inspired by his mom’s love for quiltmaking — one that guided his own path as a quilter.</p><p>“I didn't see myself as a designer, I saw myself as someone who sewed because it was a necessity, and that was something that my mom did a lot.” said Pagán-Hill. “This whole thing is a discovery for me, it’s trying to see how far I can push myself creatively.”</p><p>Frida Benitez, a graduate of the School of the Art Institute of Chicago’s fashion program, has been sewing and screen printing for about eight years. Benitez’s brand, Reina de Colores, draws inspiration from their Mexican heritage and androgynous, unisex clothing. Benitez said the show allows them to share their work with more people and immerse themselves in the local fashion scene.</p><p>“Chicago fashion is so unique, and even just like seeing people out at parties, or like drag shows, I love to see what people make and what people customize, and then even what people wear out on the street,” Benitez said. “It's really powerful, and I don't think there's any other city like it.”</p><p>Scroll down to see more images from the runway show, captured by photographer Jessie Alcheh.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Trump is gutting the Endangered Species Act, putting dozens of Illinois species at risk
entries.summary: <p>Trump administration changes to the legal interpretation of the Endangered Species Act could put 24 federally endangered species and 12 threatened species at more risk in Illinois.</p><p>Last month, the administration determined that razing the habitat where endangered or threatened species breed, feed, and shelter would no longer face federal penalties. In a separate, internal memo, the administration made clear that it also plans to reinterpret the law to only ban the intentional killing of an endangered species, letting go of the long-held criminalization of attempts to harass, harm, pursue, wound, trap, capture or collect at-risk species. (Nearly two dozen attorneys general have <a class="Link" href="https://www.courthousenews.com/almost-two-dozen-attorneys-general-sue-over-changes-to-endangered-species-act/" target="_blank" ><u>sued over some of these changes</u></a>.)</p><p>“These rule changes, when you zoom out, are an assault on threatened and endangered species unlike we've ever seen before,” said Elizabeth Forsyth, a senior attorney in the biodiversity defense program with Earthjustice. “It's an effort to eliminate habitat protections, eliminate automatic protections for threatened species, and give industry power.”</p><p>Here are three Illinois species that are now under threat:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A rusty patched bumble bee drinks nectar from a flower.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo courtesy of BeeSpotter</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h2>Rusty patched bumble bee</h2><h2></h2><p>When Libby Shafer was a biological technician with the United States Geological Survey and tried to track down the rare rusty patched bumble bee over the course of a three-month search that spanned Illinois, Indiana, and Wisconsin, she had very little luck.</p><p>“I personally only saw one,” Shafer, now an urban ecologist and PhD candidate at Northwestern University, said.</p><p>The bee, which sports a distinctive amber spot near the middle of its back, was once common in 28 states including Illinois and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The pollinator has declined by nearly <a class="Link" href="https://www.fws.gov/project/rusty-patched-bumble-bee-conservation" target="_blank" ><u>90 percent</u></a> over the past 30 years. Today, it occupies just <a class="Link" href="https://ncipmhort.cfans.umn.edu/ipm-case-studies/ipm-case-study-rusty-patched-bumble-bee" target="_blank" ><u>0.1 percent</u></a> of its historic range.</p><p>The bee was listed as federally endangered in 2017, becoming the first bee species listed under the Endangered Species Act.</p><p>The Trump administration’s reinterpretation of the Endangered Species Act could be particularly harmful to these bees because the administration will no longer consider the destruction of their habitat in violation of the law. The species is small and spends half the year in soil, making them difficult to spot for experts, let alone a developer building a road.</p><p>“This is bad news for the rusty patched bumble bee,” Schafer said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ae0000" name="image-ae0000"></a> half of all the federally endangered wildlife present in the state.</p><p>Illinois was once a hotspot for the shelled species. Scientists recorded approximately <a class="Link" href="https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/naturalist-news/2024-06-07-if-illinois-freshwater-mussels-could-talk" target="_blank" ><u>80 different species</u></a> in the state before dropping down to 59 around 1970.</p><p>Major threats to freshwater mussels include habitat degradation, water pollution, and invasive species, according to Kentaro Inoue, a research biologist at Shedd Aquarium. In Illinois and the Midwest, the species have had to contend with decades of industrial agricultural activity that have significantly altered freshwater habitats and river connectivity.</p><p>The mussels are already facing significant pressures, and the Trump administration’s rule changes won’t make their survival any easier.</p><p>“The full impact of these regulatory changes remains uncertain; however, protecting endangered mussels requires protecting not only animals themselves but also the river systems they depend on,” Inoue said.</p><p><i>This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WBEZ and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.</i></p>

entries.title: ‘Omar,’ a new American opera backed by Grammy winner Rhiannon Giddens, finally lands in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>While enslaved in North Carolina in the 1830s, Omar ibn Said wrote his story.</p><p>Scrawled in Arabic, the brief autobiography opens with passages from the Quran. It then praises God and recounts how ibn Said, a Muslim scholar, was forcibly taken from his home in West Africa and sold into slavery in the American South.</p><p>The rich text is believed to be the sole surviving Arabic-language account written by a person enslaved in the United States. But despite how rare and complex the manuscript is, it has not been widely read or taught.</p><p>That is, until Grammy Award-winning folk musician Rhiannon Giddens and composer Michael Abels, best known for his scores in movies like “Get Out” and “Us,” decided to make an opera.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Giddens, left, and Abels won the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Music for their work “Omar.” “His story needs to be known. People are beginning to wake up to the fact that he existed and find value in his story,” Abels said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Associated Press</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>ibn Said’s story powers the Pulitzer Prize-winning opera “<a class="Link" href="https://www.lyricopera.org/shows/upcoming/2026-27/Omar/" target="_blank" ><u>Omar</u></a>,” which will open for a short run this week at Chicago’s Lyric Opera, a co-commissioner of the work. As the show makes its long-awaited Midwest debut, Lyric leadership is encouraging Chicagoans to <a class="Link" href="https://www.lyricopera.org/lyric-lately/chicago-reads-omar/" target="_blank" ><u>read the original text</u></a> and says it’s the exact right time to present this deeply American story.</p><p>When the heavyweight creative duo began working on the project in 2018, neither Giddens — a folk musician who is herself a trained opera singer — nor Abels had ever heard of ibn Said. South Carolina’s Spoleto Festival USA, a leading Southern cultural series that takes place each spring, brought the idea to Giddens, who enlisted Abels.</p><p>“His story needs to be known,” Abels said. “And people are beginning to wake up to the fact that he existed and find value in his story.”</p><p>Since its world premiere in 2022, “Omar” has been widely praised, including with the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Music. But it has taken some time to wind its way to Chicago, after stops in Los Angeles, San Francisco and Boston, arriving here as the country marks its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/04/02/america-250-illinois-chicago-federal-national-endowment-arts-trump" target="_blank" ><u>250th anniversary</u></a>. Lyric’s President and CEO <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2024/10/28/john-mangum-lyric-opera-ceo-chicago-houston-symphony" target="_blank" ><u>John Mangum</u></a> said it’s a fitting moment to present this “only in America kind of work.”</p><p>“I feel like there's a bit of a paradox, but there's no better way to celebrate the history of our country than by confronting it honestly,” Mangum said. “And I think this is a work of art that confronts the history of our country and the impact of slavery.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div All three are appearing in the show for the first time.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Leah Wellman/Lyric Opera of Chicago</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><a class="Link" href="https://www.lyricopera.org/shows/upcoming/2026-27/Omar/" target="_blank" ><u>Omar</u></a><br><b>When:</b> Oct. 23-28<br><b>Where:</b> Lyric Opera House, 20 N. Wacker Drive<br><b>Info:</b> Tickets from $75</div> </div><p>At Lyric, the titular role will be played by tenor Issachah Savage, who will be joined on stage by soprano Kearstin Piper Brown as Julie, a fictional enslaved woman who helps Omar. Hometown mezzo-soprano <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2024/11/17/blue-review-lyric-opera-chicago-tazewell-thompson-jeanine-tesori-kenneth-kellogg-zoie-reams" target="_blank" ><u>Zoie Reams</u></a> will perform the role of Fatima, Omar’s mother. All three are appearing in the show for the first time.</p><p>Despite Giddens’ involvement, the show is not simply a folk score adapted for the operatic stage. In fact, Giddens’ signature instrument, the banjo, is not used at all.</p><p>“Rhiannon likes to say the orchestra is the banjo, and that is actually a lot of how the orchestration works,” Abels said. “The opera is a perfect excuse to use all the different forms of American music that is really music from elsewhere, but we think of as American. And music that we don't think of as American, but really is.”</p><p>In Chicago, “Omar” will have just three performances (as compared to the eight for the Lyric’s season opener, Mozart’s “Don Giovanni”). Mangum said the programming decision was based on lower demand in recent seasons for contemporary titles, although he said this show was “selling very well.”</p><p>Beyond the stage, Lyric has teamed up with other local arts organizations, museums and universities to <a class="Link" href="https://www.lyricopera.org/lyric-lately/chicago-reads-omar/" target="_blank" ><u>encourage Chicagoans</u></a> to read ibn Said’s original text through a translation available on the Library of Congress’ <a class="Link" href="https://www.loc.gov/resource/amedsaid1831.dw027/?sp=1&st=image" target="_blank" ><u>website</u></a>. The Library purchased ibn Said’s original manuscript in 2017, after it spent decades in private collections.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> But unlike ibn Said’s account, written while he was still enslaved in North Carolina, most of those were written by individuals after they were freed, since most enslaved people were barred from learning to read or write.</p><p>“Omar's account is really a sort of unbelievable survival and an amazing witness, and we don't have a lot of accounts like that,” said Newberry’s Will Hansen, who curates the collection that includes plantation and genealogical records from the period of slavery.</p><p>“It is an important reminder to us how complex and rich American history is,” Hansen said. “Many people don't think about practicing Muslims living in North Carolina in the first half of the 19th century, but they are there, and Omar proves that.”</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Despite Giddens’ involvement, “Omar” is not simply a folk score adapted for the operatic stage. In fact, Giddens’ signature instrument, the banjo, is not used at all.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Amy Harris/Amy Harris/Invision/Associated Press</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>ibn Said’s work is cautious and, despite nods to his Muslim faith, it also cites the Bible (his enslaver, James Owen, had given him a Bible written in Arabic in an attempt to convert ibn Said to Christianity). The text is also overly gracious to the Owen family, who held him as property. As composer Michael Abels put it, “the autobiography is very telling in the things it doesn't say.”</p><p>“Omar's biography is not a juicy tell-all in any way, and it occurs to me that maybe if I was in fear for my life and enslaved, I might be a bit hesitant to speak my mind,” Abels said.</p><p>Still, Abels said, there is something about ibn Said’s story that continues to resonate, nearly 200 years after it was written.</p><p>“It's a story of a strange person in a strange land,” Abels said. “Omar walks among us, and there are people whose stories, in the tiny details, are different than Omar's, but overall are exactly Omar's story today. Now more than ever, this story needs to be told.”</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: Envy gets a bad rap. Here's how this basketball player turned the toxic emotion on its head.
entries.summary: <p>It was supposed to be Brooks Barnhizer’s year.</p><p>Barnhizer, a junior at Northwestern in 2023, was second on Northwestern University’s basketball team only to its star senior, Boo Buie. Boo was the attention-grabbing guard, making game-winning shots at the buzzer. Brooks was an all-around solid player who “stuffed the stat sheet” with points, rebounds, steals, assists, and blocks. Together, they took Northwestern University’s Men’s team to the NCAA Tournament for only the third time in the school’s history.</p><p>At the start of the 2024–25 season, all eyes were on Brooks to lead the team. The goal was not just to get back to the tournament, but to make school history and win more games there. He was prepared. Between seasons, he practiced with the team Monday through Friday, then hopped on a plane to New Jersey for extra workouts with NBA trainers Friday night, twice Saturday, and Sunday before flying back to Evanston.</p><p>“He is one of the hardest-working players I have ever coached,” said assistant coach Brian James, who retired from Northwestern this past June.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Northwestern head coach Chris Collins (left) talks to guard Brooks Barnhizer during March Madness in 2024. Halfway through Barnhizer’s senior year on the team, Collins tearfully announced that Brooks was out with an injury for the rest of the 2024-25 season. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Nam Y. Huh/AP Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Brooks’s highly anticipated return was delayed, however, due to a summer injury to his foot, forcing him to sit out the first few games of the season to rehab instead.</p><p>On February 1, 2025, after playing 17 games and averaging 17.1 points per game, Brooks didn’t suit up. At the post-game press conference, Northwestern head coach Chris Collins couldn’t hold back tears as he announced that Brooks was out for the season.</p><p>Brooks had reinjured his foot five games prior. Despite needing surgery, he had not wanted to end his college career just yet. “Being the way Brooks is, he begged me to play . . . He said, ‘I gotta put the jersey on one more time,’” Collins said. After playing well in the game following the injury, they had decided to take it game by game.</p><p>Eventually, Coach Collins asked Brooks to help Nick Martinelli, the team’s forward, learn how to run a team. “I put Brooks in charge . . . to be Nick’s whisperer . . . to be there every game, and be that strong voice and be that person who Nick sees to help him . . . becoming a star player,” Collins said.</p><p>It was supposed to be Brooks’s year. And then it wasn’t. It was Nick’s.</p><h3><b>The silent operator</b></h3><p>Put simply, envy is wanting what someone else has. While we all feel envy, we don’t talk about it. Not only is it unpleasant, but it’s also socially unacceptable.</p><p>Most people believe that the problem of envy is that it is inherently evil, that it ignites greed and hate and can cause people to steal, slander, or become violent.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a80000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In a new book out Oct. 20, 2026, <a class="Link" href="https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/stacy-s-kim-ph-d/envy/9781668659939/?lens=balance" target="_blank" >“Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want,”</a> author Stacy S. Kim argues that the toxic emotion can be harnessed for good. “Envy can be the poison that flows from toxic comparisons or a potion that reveals purpose and connection,” Kim writes. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Lisa Hancock (Kim)</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The real problem of envy, however, is that we are oblivious to how much and how often it operates in our lives and that we allow this to happen. It slips in, makes us feel uncomfortable, so we avoid or ignore it.</p><p>Doing so, we allow it to influence our thoughts and behavior. When we bottle up our negative emotions, they tend to seep out but in unexpected, uncontrollable, and unwanted ways.</p><p>I want to flip the switch on envy: Envy can be the poison that flows from toxic comparisons or a potion that reveals purpose and connection. You can dismiss envy as something bad, or you can examine your envy and harness it for good.</p><h3><b>Envy in sports</b></h3><p>Sports is not only a breeding ground for envy, but it also offers us public examples to see the many ways in which envy can operate in anyone’s life.</p><p>This is because contrasts are easy to make in sports. Envy is a result of making upward comparisons. If you have a lot of opportunities or the tendency to juxtapose your situation against someone else’s, you’re more likely to find instances when you’re behind and hence feel envy. In sports, the physical abilities of its players are measurable in concrete terms, and the competition between players and teams is on display for all to see.</p><p>“Differences are so obvious. In other domains, not so, but in sports, comparisons are harder to escape, especially in a context where the people involved are experts,” said Sara Protasi, a philosophy professor at the University of Puget Sound who studies envy.</p><p>Moreover, every sport has defined rules for behavior, space boundaries, and time limits. Perhaps this is why a bit of rivalry, physical force, and ambition in sports are socially acceptable and not hidden from view but sometimes even celebrated.</p><p>Sports therefore offer us examples of envy in plain sight so we can see just how insidious its power can be, not just for evil but for good. And here is where Brooks Barnhizer comes in. His story highlights different ways to respond to envy, making them easier to see.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e90000" name="image-e90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Northwestern guard Brooks Barnhizer during the second half of an NCAA college basketball game that Northwestern won 70-66 in overtime Friday, Dec. 6, 2024, in Evanston.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Erin Hooley/AP Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Early challenges in Irvington, Alabama </b></h3><p>Brooks started playing basketball early and often. Not only was he born in Indiana, where kids begin playing soon after walking, he was born to a renowned high school basketball coach, Mark Barnhizer. Both he and his older brother, Braxton, grew up in the gym starting at 5:30 a.m. every morning, including Christmas.</p><p>“The boys would wake up Christmas morning, and they would want to go shoot. Their Christmas morning workouts were fun times because nobody else was in the gym,” said Heidi Barnhizer, Brooks’s mom.</p><p>When Brooks was in the seventh grade and Braxton in eighth, his dad was offered a job coaching basketball at Alma Bryant High School in Irvington, Alabama. Mark Barnhizer agreed to take the job only after he learned that Alabama was one of a handful of states that allowed middle-schoolers to play varsity.</p><p>The plan was for Brooks to wait a year and play JV before joining the high school team. When the family arrived, however, the program was worse off than expected. Coach Barnhizer had both of his sons play.</p><p>The other boys at the school were not happy.</p><p>“‘You’re on the team because your dad’s the coach.’ Yeah, that’s what they said . . . to my face,” Brooks recalled. “Seventh graders usually don’t play up, so it was definitely a challenge.”</p><h3><b>Four components of envy </b></h3><p>Now we need to understand how envy is built. I found it helpful to identify what I see as four key components.</p><p>First, someone else not so far off from the envier possesses the thing the envier wants. This “similar target” is someone within reach of the envier. We often envy our classmates, friends and co-workers, and not teachers, strangers or bosses.</p><p>Second, the envier picks a domain that is important to him or her. This “relevant comparison” often happens so quickly, the envier isn’t always aware. The boys who envied Brooks the most were likely to be the ones who played basketball.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9d0000" name="image-9d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b7d4a6a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4550x2554+0+240/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2Fa9%2Fe2086022409499268d1368abe40b%2Fillinois-northwestern-basketball.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/703c77e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4550x2554+0+240/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2Fa9%2Fe2086022409499268d1368abe40b%2Fillinois-northwestern-basketball.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8f6a78c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4550x2554+0+240/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2Fa9%2Fe2086022409499268d1368abe40b%2Fillinois-northwestern-basketball.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Northwestern forward Nick Martinelli became the object of Barnhizer’s mentoring in 2025. Martinelli ended the season as the leading scorer in the Big Ten Conference and for Northwestern Men’s Basketball.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Erin Hooley/AP Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Third, envy reveals what we want. But here is where we often go wrong. We assume envy involves wanting things we can see, like beauty or money. The core of our longing, however, is “intangible desire” — what we feel.</p><p>Finally, the envier experiences an ache, pain or discomfort. These “negative emotions” stem from both the lack of what is wanted and the sense of inferiority from the comparison. It can also make us feel guilty or embarrassed and want to suppress or deny the feeling.</p><p>If we were to map these components of envy, it might be as follows: The boys saw Brooks, a new kid at school (similar target), play some ball during PE and expected to compete against him in try-outs for the middle school team (relevant comparison). The boys who tried out wanted to be a part of the team (intangible desire). But when they saw Brooks make the high-school team, they felt the pain of inferiority and unfairness (negative emotion). They gossiped and didn’t respond well.</p><h3><b>Flipping the switch </b></h3><p>Meanwhile, Brooks had a more useful response to his own envy. Specifically, how he started loving basketball was a moment of envy.</p><p>“The earliest memory of me loving the game wasn’t me playing. It was me watching. Watching my dad coach, watching the players that play for him play. I loved how competitive it was,” Brooks said.</p><p>“Whenever he would lose, I would always get, not sad, but mad, like ‘When I grow up and play for him, we’re not ever going to lose. I don’t ever want him to lose,’” he said. Brooks felt both envious and jealous of the boys who played for his dad.</p><p>During that first year playing as a seventh grader for his dad’s high school team, when Brooks sensed others’ animosity, he kept his focus on basketball. “It made me grow closer not only to my family but also to the game. I had to prove that first game that I belonged,” he said.</p><p>The hard work paid off. “I scored seventeen points,” he said. “And it was funny, by halfway through that year, everybody was probably, like my biggest fan in the town, and our team was like, good again.”</p><p>Brooks managed his emotions in a similar way when sidelined in 2025: His focus of concern was again on basketball and what he loved and wanted, rather than on Nick Martinelli, the target of his envy. He saw helping Nick as a way to practice a new skill — coaching. He saw mentoring Nick as a way to continue to be a part of the game he loves and practice what he might do later. So when Nick succeeded, it meant he had, too.</p><p>Nick Martinelli responded by becoming the leading scorer in the Big Ten Conference and Northwestern Men’s Basketball season.</p><p>Brooks harnessed his envy for good.</p><p><i>Both now play in the NBA, Barnhizer for the Oklahoma City Thunder and Martinelli for the Los Angeles Clippers. </i></p><hr><p>Excerpted from <a class="Link" href="https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/stacy-s-kim-ph-d/envy/9781538776735/?lens=balance" target="_blank" >“Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want”</a> by Stacy S. Kim, PhD. Copyright © 2026 by Stacy S. Kim, PhD. Reprinted with permission of Balance Publishing, an imprint of Hachette Book Group. All rights reserved.</p>

entries.title: One of buzziest titles at Chicago International Film Fest is a comedic thriller by a Chicago ad director
entries.summary: <p>Whether it's binging distressing documentaries or falling asleep to grisly podcasts, many of us are obsessed with true crime.</p><p>But could we actually solve a real-life murder on our own?</p><p>That’s a question explored by “Ana the Cleaner,” the debut feature film from Chicago commercial director Guy Bauer. The namesake protagonist is a Ukrainian immigrant and housekeeper who listens to the “True Crime and Killer Wine” podcast while cleaning the ritzy homes of wealthy Chicagoans. When a creepy client’s wife disappears, she launches an amateur investigation with the help of her quirky friends and family.</p><p>Shot in the city and surrounding suburbs, the comedic thriller sold out its premiere last week in the opening days of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/15/chicago-international-film-festival-celebrity-movie-red-carpet-john-c-reilly-derrick-rose" >Chicago International Film Festival</a>. Nominated for the event’s Chicago Award, it will screen again on Wednesday and get a third screening Saturday at AMC Newcity. (Tickets for Saturday’s showing go on sale at 9 a.m. Tuesday at <a class="Link" href="http://chicagofilmfestival.com" target="_blank" ><u>chicagofilmfestival.com</u></a>.)</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chicago-based director Guy Bauer poses on the red carpet at the premiere of his self-financed film, “Ana the Cleaner,” during the 62nd Chicago International Film Festival. “After spending 16 years making commercials and branded films, I decided it was time to put my own money into telling a story of my own,” he said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The movie is gaining momentum, with forthcoming screenings at the St. Louis International Film Festival and FilmQuest’s Utah-based Marché du Cthulhu event. Bauer hopes it will catch the eye of distributors and expand his career beyond advertising projects, which have narrative limitations.</p><p>“My feedback [from clients] is always like, ‘Make it shorter. Less story. Just show the product,’” said Bauer, founder of the Umault ad agency in Oakbrook Terrace.</p><p>But “Ana the Cleaner” was “a breath of fresh air,” he said.</p><p>“Finally, I feel like this is where I belong.”</p><p>Bauer financed the film independently through his agency and shot footage in Oak Park, Barrington and other areas in and near Chicago. He completed principal photography in just 16 days, from late February to early March.</p><p>"After spending 16 years making commercials and branded films, I decided it was time to put my own money into telling a story of my own," he said. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/IZYOoEkbly4?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="ANA THE CLEANER | Official Trailer | Competent Pictures"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>The movie balances a suspense-building plot with character development and plenty of humor. In one scene, included in the trailer, Ana has a nightmare after dozing off to a true crime podcast. But an advertisement hilariously intrudes into the dream, cutting it short.</p><p>Bauer said he wants viewers to relate to moments like those in the film.</p><p>“The essence of entertaining someone is to show them to themselves, like you're not alone,” he said.</p><p>More laughs are generated by the conversations Ana, portrayed by Yana Roykhman, has with her sister, Inna (Ilana Kohanchi); Ned, Inna’s partner (Caleb Harbin); and Ted, a friend harboring a crush (Connor Green).</p><p>Roykhman said having a good time was the top priority during the fast-paced shoot.</p><p>“It was like the first thing we talked about,” said Roykhman, who is from Ukraine and lives in Los Angeles. “It doesn't matter if it's going to be difficult or if we're going to be exhausted. We're going to have fun.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-420000" viewers on the war in Ukraine – even through small bits of dialogue in the film.</p><p>“It was such an honor for me to be in that movie and represent Ukrainian people and talk more about what's going on in my country,” she said.</p><p>Unlike other out-of-town actors, Roykhman said she welcomed Chicago’s grueling weather.</p><p>“In one month, I experienced rain, hail and snow,” she said. “I miss snow so much.”</p><p>Roykhman also said she was grateful for the city’s “support.”</p><p>Bauer is hoping the hometown love will propel the film to further success.</p><p>“It starts with Chicago,” he entries.title: Woman sues University of Chicago fraternity chapter over reported sexual assault
entries.summary: <p>A woman sued a University of Chicago fraternity Tuesday alleging she was raped earlier this year by one of its members.</p><p>The lawsuit, filed Monday in Cook County court, holds that a member of Alpha Delta Phi sexually assaulted the 19-year-old woman during a fraternity party on Feb. 7. The woman is identified only as "Jane Doe."</p><p>The lawsuit comes just over a week after the Chicago Police Department opened an investigation into another report of<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" target="_blank" ><u> sexual assault at a fraternity party</u></a> at the University of Chicago chapter of Alpha Epsilon Pi.</p><p>Jane Doe's lawsuit points to a history of police investigations into sexual assault reports tied to the university's Alpha Delta Phi fraternity chapter.</p><p>The lawsuit says that a fraternity member gave Jane Doe a shot of alcohol and she was later found unconscious in a room. A friend found her and helped her leave the house, but she struggled to speak and walk as she was led out, according to the suit. </p><p>The next morning, Jane Doe discovered bloodstains in her underwear and reported the alleged assault to Chicago police.</p><p>That investigation remains open, according to the lawsuit.</p><p>The lawsuit accuses Alpha Delta Phi and its University of Chicago chapter of ignoring sexual assault allegations against members and failing to “put meaningful safeguards in place.”</p><p>The University of Chicago and Alpha Delta Phi didn't respond to requests for comment.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/12/woman-21-sexually-assaulted-near-the-university-of-chicago-in-hyde-park" >UChicago frat suspends events after report of sexual assault; students question campus training, Greek life</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >Group cheered as woman was sexually assaulted at University of Chicago frat house, police report says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/14/university-of-chicago-sexual" >No arrests in wake of reported sexual assault at University of Chicago frat house, police say</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Feud between progressive unions that put Mayor Johnson in office yields Giannoulias key endorsement
entries.summary: <p>The long-simmering feud between Mayor Brandon Johnson and half of the coalition of progressive unions that helped put him in office boiled over Tuesday, triggering a pivotal endorsement for Illlinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias in the race for mayor.</p><p>Service Employees International Union Locals 1 and 73 threw their formidable support behind Giannoulias, the presumed frontrunner with a campaign war chest of $19.2 million. SEIU affiliates together contributed over $4.5 million to Johnson’s 2023 mayoral campaign. The union also provided scores of campaign workers and materials.</p><p>Those resources will now presumably be available to Giannoulias — and more importantly, denied to Johnson, who has just $379,471 in cash on hand.</p><p>SEIU’s decision to divorce itself from Johnson comes as no surprise, and has been building since early 2025.</p><p>That’s when SEIU accused the Chicago Teachers Union of crafting contract proposals that would train teacher assistants to do work currently done by members of SEIU Local 73, potentially diminishing the union’s future ranks. SEIU Local 73 went so far as to sign onto an internal SEIU-wide resolution declaring itself “under attack” by CTU.</p><p>The conflict was ultimately resolved — with a CTU retreat on the job raid issue and a new teachers contract that included an increase in the number of teaching assistants as well as job protections for them.</p><p>Nevertheless, the damage was done. Trust was broken — and so was the once powerful coalition of progressive unions that helped put Johnson in office.</p><p>Johnson is a former middle school teacher who served as a paid organizer for CTU before becoming mayor. But SEIU expected mayoral neutrality on the job raid issue — and they didn't get it from Johnson.</p><p>“I understand relationships. I asked him to stand down," Local 73 President Dian Palmer told the Sun-Times. "We had all kinds of evidence that these workers belonged to us. I told him, `You don’t have to do anything. These are your friends. Just let us go through the grievance process.’ He told me that he would call me back and he never called me back.” </p><p>“That was hurtful. I felt like we were fighting for our labor life because this unit is one of the larger units that we have and it would change our life tremendously if we were to lose these members.”</p><p>Another item on SEIU’s bill of particulars was the mayor’s decision to join forces with CTU in pressuring the board to take out a high-interest loan to reimburse the city for a $175 million pension payment for non-teaching school employees that ultimately triggered the firing of Chicago Public Schools CEO Pedro Martinez.</p><p>Martinez's replacement, Macquline King, also refused to take out the loan and instead pushed through a budget that assumes a $150 million increase in state funding.</p><p>“When the loan happens and people don’t have the money to [make payments] they pick the low-hanging fruit. They’re not gonna get rid of teachers. So they start to get rid of ancillary staff. That would be our members,” Palmer said.</p><p>The rift between CTU and SEIU prompted the former allies to endorse rival candidates in races for seats on the soon-to-be elected school board, including board presidents. </p><p>Anthony Driver took a leave of absence as executive director of SEIU's Illinois State Council to chair of a new SEIU-funded PAC Brighter Futures to help elect SEIU-backed candidates to the new 21-member board, including board president candidate Jessica Biggs.</p><p>Palmer, who has worked with Giannoulias and endorsed him for Illinois Secretary of State, said her members believe they have a politician they can trust to at least remain neutral if a similar controversy arises.</p><p>Together, the three SEIU locals represent 50,000 Chicago employees. Thousands of them are private sector janitors and custodians employed by city contractors. Local 73 alone represents 18,000 government employees, most of them at CPS. </p><p>“Alexi will be fairer because he doesn’t have the kind of relationships with people that Brandon did,” Palmer said of CTU. “We had a mayor who we had done everything to get elected both financially, physically, canvassing, everything. And then, on the one opportunity that he had — where he didn’t have to do anything, just stay out of it and say, `Both of you are my friends. I’m hoping you all work it out. If you want me to come in and mediate this, I will. But otherwise, I’m not gonna get involved in it.’ But, he didn’t.”</p><p>Senior mayoral adviser Jason Lee said Johnson’s “record of standing up for working people speaks for itself" and he will take his case directly to SEIU members.</p><p>“Political alliances are always shifting… You want as much support as you can get. But what this election is going to come down to is the records of the individual candidates,” he said. “Members of various unions who live in the city, get up every day trying to put food on the table — those voters are gonna look at the records of the candidates. The mayor feels very strongly and confident that his record will hold up against anybody else in the field.”<br></p>

entries.title: Charges pending for suspect who fired shots near Loop's Kluczynski Federal Building
entries.summary: <p>One person was taken into custody early Tuesday after firing shots, causing damage to a building in the Loop near the Kluczynski Federal Building. </p><p>At 4:30 a.m., someone saw a gunman shooting in the 200 block of South Dearborn Street, police said. </p><p>No one was shot or injured but a nearby building in the Dearborn Street address was damaged, police said. </p><p>Charges are pending for the gunman, who police arrested on the scene. A gun was also recovered. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating.<br></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydijldty-l-t/" target="_blank" >Mayoral race revs up as candidates file stacks of nominating petitions</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydijldty-l-i/" target="_blank" >Mariah Woelfel</a></h5><p><b>How they stack up</b>: Mayoral contenders on Monday brought tall stacks of nominating petitions to the downtown Chicago Board of Elections office, where election workers measured the stacks with wooden rulers. It marked the start of the weeklong filing period for February's election, intended to whittle down the crowded mayoral race by cutting from the ballot candidates who fail to collect at least 12,500 valid petition signatures. Officials will certify all candidates on the ballot by Dec. 17.</p><p><b>Signature move</b>: Mayor, city treasurer and city clerk candidates often turn in double or triple the number of signatures needed to be safe from validity challenges. Mayoral candidate and businessman Willie Wilson said he plans to challenge "everyone."</p><p><b>Chicago tradition</b>: Candidates who turn in their signatures first thing Monday get entered into a lottery for the coveted first spot on the ballot. Others may wait to file on the last day, Oct. 26, for a chance at the last place on the ballot. It's all to avoid being an overlooked name in the middle of a pack and reel in any uninformed voters who might check the easiest box.</p><p><b>Mayoral candidate standings</b>: Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias said he submitted 60,000 signatures. John Kelly estimated he turned in more than 36,000. Wilson turned in an estimated 35,000. Matt Brewer, a commissioner on the Chicago Housing Authority board, said he submitted "over 32,000." Spokespeople for Mayor Brandon Johnson and Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza, both absent Monday, said they plan to file later.</p><p><a class="Link" class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydijldty-l-z/" target="_blank" >Kaitlin Washburn</a></h5><p><b>At risk</b>: Changes by President Donald Trump's administration to the legal interpretation of the Endangered Species Act could put 24 federally endangered species and 12 threatened species at greater risk in Illinois. That includes the rusty patched bumble bee, piping plovers and freshwater mussels.</p><p><b>What has changed</b>: Last month, the administration determined that those razing the habitat where endangered or threatened species breed, feed and shelter would no longer face federal penalties. Lightbody, life’s a period piece</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydijldty-l-ty/" target="_blank" >Selena Fragassi</a></h5><p>In Chicago, V.V. Lightbody (whose real name is Vivian McConnell) is permanently on the indie rock speed dial, called upon any time a band gets a craving for some extra wind instruments.</p><p>She has worked with Twin Peaks, Whitney, Finom and Elizabeth Moen. And demand is not just among Chicago musicians — let's not forget Harry Styles.</p><p>"That was a crazy one-off scenario," she said of filling in for his gig at the BBC Radio One's Big Weekend Festival in 2022, also contributing keys, guitar and vocals, all of which she is equally versed in.</p><p>But after years of supporting other musicians, including being a proud "album doula" in the studio, Lightbody is finally back with her first proper solo album in six years: "Period Piece," released Oct. 9.</p><p>"In these songs, I'm thinking deeply and feeling the world pretty heavily," Lightbody told the Sun-Times. "You feel the pressure of a person who's trying to live, but that feels really exciting to me."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydijldty-l-tj/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What are your home remedies when you're feeling under the weather? 🤧</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Safety repairs cause temporary closure of Midway Airport runway
entries.summary: <p>A runway at Midway International Airport is closed through mid-November so crews can perform safety repairs, the city announced.</p><p>Runway 22L is closed to arrivals and departures effective immediately while repairs are made for recent damages caused by aircraft activity, the Chicago Department of Aviation announced. </p><p>"Safety is the top priority at Chicago’s airports, and we are working to complete these repairs safely and promptly,” said CDA Commissioner Michael McMurray. “We’re coordinating closely with our partners at the FAA and the airlines to reduce disruptions for travelers and return the airfield to normal operating conditions as quickly and safely as possible.”</p><p>The department says cancellations and delays are possible due to the closure, but that the extent of those disruptions will depend on airline schedules and weather conditions. </p>

entries.title: Boy, 17, shot in Englewood dies
entries.summary: <p>A 17-year-old boy shot in Englewood on Monday morning has died, officials said. </p><p>The unidentified boy, 17, was walking in the 800 block of West 71st Street about 11 a.m. when two gunmen confronted him brandishing guns and shot in his direction, hitting him about the body, police said. </p><p>The boy was taken to the University of Chicago Hospital in critical condition but he later died, according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>No other injuries were reported. </p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson renews fight for his failed corporate head tax
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is resurrecting his failed corporate head tax and proposing his third and biggest increase yet in a tax on equipment rentals and cloud computing that is already the highest in the nation.</p><p>The spending plan that will serve as Johnson’s re-election platform also seeks to nearly double the tax on sports betting, from 10.25% to match the current amusement tax to 20%. </p><p>By renewing his bid to impose a corporate head tax, Johnson is defying the line in the sand drawn by the coalition of conservative and moderate Council members who rejected the head tax a year ago.</p><p>In a letter to the mayor last month, 29 alderpersons established three boundary lines for the pre-election budget debate: no property tax increase, no “head tax or tax on job growth” and no counting on money from Springfield not yet approved.</p><p>Johnson is following two out of three of those guidelines by freezing property taxes and assuming no help from the state.</p><p>But he’s setting aside the most important boundary — by triggering another bitter battle for the head tax that his entrenched opposition has essentially declared “dead on arrival.”</p><p>To generate $101 million in annual revenue, Johnson’s latest version of the corporate head tax would be imposed at a rate of $25 a month per employee on businesses with more than 125 employees. That amounts to just 2.8% of registered corporations, according to the mayor’s office.</p><p>Last year’s version of the head tax was repeatedly revised and finally landed at a rate of $33 per employee on companies with 100 or more workers. In an apparent attempt to soften the blow, the Johnson administration is pairing the new version of the head tax with a tax credit.</p><p>It would allow employers whose work sites are located within Chicago census tracts designated as “socio-economically disadvantaged areas” to apply for a “full rebate” of the head tax. He's also branding the per-worker levy an “Equitable Employer Tax.”</p><p></p><p>No matter what the mayor calls it, business leaders who bankrolled last year's big bucks battle over the head tax likely will characterize Johnson's measure as a job killer.</p><p>But it will at least allow the embattled mayor to connect with the progressive base of voters who helped put him in office, and say that he went down fighting for a budget that requires corporations to “pay their fair share.”</p><p>“There’s greater evidence of working people being pushed out of the city of Chicago than any sort of claim of the possibility of a business leaving Chicago. Working people are being forced out of cities across America. Corporations are not,” Johnson told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“As the wealth gap between CEOs and working people continues to spread, we have to decide what’s most important. Is it protection of a tiny, tiny, less than one-tenth of a percentage? Or is it worthwhile protecting families that are paying more in gas and groceries and rent than they’ve had to pay in a lifetime?”</p><p>The head tax will serve as Ground Zero for the budget battle, but Johnson is relying more heavily on a personal property lease transaction tax that has turned into a cash cow for Chicago.</p><p>It’s also been one of the few business taxes that Johnson has been able to raise with minimal resistance from the business community and the coalition of opposition alderpersons that he calls the “Corporate Caucus.”</p><p>The tax applies to businesses and individuals who lease personal property, software or cloud services. That includes everything from equipment, furniture and vehicles to movies and streaming services.</p><p>To generate an additional $234 million in 2027, the PPLT would rise by a whopping 33%. The tax now imposed at a rate of 15% would increase by five full percentage points — to 20%.</p><p>To soften the blow for everyday consumers, the PPLT that applies to car leasing would remain at 15%. Film and television crews using Chicago as a backdrop would get a break — from 15% currently to 11% to incentivize local productions.</p><p>“The PPLT has over-performed this year, bringing in hundreds of millions of dollars. And we remained the top destination for corporate relocation in the country,” Johnson said.</p><p>“This tax is gonna provide a lower rate for our film industry and it’s gonna keep the vehicle rate steady so people who are leasing vehicles won’t see an increase. But we are talking about these corporations that are experiencing rapid growth, with worldwide software expected to reach $1.4 trillion in 2026 alone… We’re talking about Google, Amazon, Salesforce. These big corporations that are making hundreds of billions of dollars in terms of profit margins. What we are expecting them to do is pay their fair share.”</p><p>The mayor’s budget also seeks to nearly double the tax on sports betting — from 10.25% to match the city’s amusement tax of 20%.</p><p>That’s expected to generate roughly $37 million in annual revenue. But only if it survives an ongoing court challenge by the Sports Betting Alliance made up of major sportsbooks like FanDuel and DraftKings.</p><p>“This is revenue that is generated from the companies — not the actual bettors. The additional revenue is not a direct charge to Chicagoans placing bets. It’s actually on the companies,” Johnson said.</p><p>Major sportsbooks have an ongoing lawsuit against the city, arguing that the authority for regulating and taxing sports betting rests exclusively with the state.</p><p>Last year, 30 Illinois House Democrats urged the City Council to spike Johnson’s proposal to tax online sports betting for fear that it would invite other municipalities to do the same, drive online sports betting underground and send state revenue on a tailspin.</p><p>To avert yet another point of political contention, the mayor’s budget will earmark $360 million for an advanced pension payment over and above the $2.79 billion statutorily required by law.</p><p>Last year, Johnson tried to cut the pension advance in half — only to restore it, delay it and ultimately make the full $260 million advanced pension payment after his City Council opponents demanded it.</p><p>Johnson is expected to deliver his fourth budget message to the City Council Wednesday.</p><p>That will be followed by two weeks of budget hearings that will give anti-administration alderpersons a forum to interrogate what has been a revolving door of city department heads.</p><p>By renewing his fight for a corporate head tax, Johnson is all but inviting another marathon budget stalemate.</p><p>Retiring Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th) is already predicting a “long, protracted, ugly budget season” that could drag on “right up to the deadline or even past it.”</p><p>Although Johnson got away with raising the so-called cloud tax for two years straight, O’Shea argued that the tax is now at the breaking point.</p><p>“Where we are now is the highest anywhere in the country. He wants to go even higher… You can’t keep going back to the same well. You can’t keep raising a tax that’s gonna hurt people who work out of their homes in addition to successful businesses,” O’Shea said.</p><p>“I’m very concerned that, if this goes up again, we’re gonna see a backlash. We’re gonna see people looking for other ways to avoid this.”</p><p>Pressed to identify his fallback if the head tax is once again rejected, the mayor would only say that he would “evaluate all of our revenue options” to bankroll what he called “investments that need to be made to support working people.”</p><p>“The most important part of this budget is ensuring that we’re investing in our young people. That we’re investing in our libraries. That we’re investing in community violence intervention workers who have demonstrated that their presence drives violence down,” Johnson said. “What we do know to be a job killer is when we disinvest on the West and South Sides of Chicago.”</p>

entries.title: Little Village won the White West, so why hasn't CPS promoted them to the prestigious Red conference?
entries.summary: <p>Dion Boyd Jr. put the work in throughout his high school basketball career. The four-year starter is a key part of Little Village’s remarkable rise in Public League basketball.</p><p>Little Village won the Blue West in 2024-25 and flew through the White West last season with an undefeated conference record and a 27-7 overall season.</p><p>But when Chicago Public Schools revealed the basketball conference alignments for the upcoming season, Little Village was not promoted to the Red.</p><p>“I put in a lot of hours over the years,” Boyd told the Sun-Times. “Early mornings, late practices, extra work in the gym. I took it seriously and helped the team keep moving forward.”</p><p>Traditionally, teams that win White conferences are promoted to the Red. But the Public League <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/2026/10/13/chicago-public-league-basketball-cps" >expanded the Red</a> from 32 to 40 teams this season. Prosser and Wells were elevated from the White West to the Red West. But Little Village was not.</p><p>“My goal was always to reach the Red Conference by my senior year,” Boyd said. “That was what I was working toward the whole time. Finding out CPS isn’t promoting us and we’re being held back hit hard. After all the time and effort we put in to climb from Blue to White, it feels like we got stopped right when we were about to make it to the top. I wanted to finish my high school career competing in the Red Conference, but that chance is gone now.”</p><p>According to former Little Village basketball coach Chris Presswood, the Public League is punishing Little Village over a player who transferred from Juarez to Little Village last season.</p><p>“The Juarez coach made a big deal about it, but both principals agreed it was a transfer for his living situation,” Presswood said. “I reached out to Juarez’s coach and let him know that the kid didn’t want to leave. He was a starter at Juarez. He was the man there, and he was barely going to play here.”</p><p>Neither CPS nor the IHSA forced Little Village to forfeit any games from last season. But CPS confirmed Tuesday that Little Village was denied promotion to the Red because of a transfer-eligibility issue.</p><p>Presswood says there was a mix-up where CPS sent an email to Juarez’s old athletic director instead of the new one for the final paperwork.</p><p>“If they had just updated the email, everything would have been fine,” Presswood said. “They know what they did. The IHSA didn’t see any tampering and [the player] was ruled eligible. I’ve been raising hell about this since it happened, but no one cares because it is Little Village and it doesn’t affect them. But it affects my kids. They worked hard for that.</p><p>“CPS is a joke. The way they are moving, they are just trying to keep everything hush-hush.”</p><p>According to Presswood, the transfer player from Juarez averaged “maybe two points and had no minutes in meaningful games.”</p><p>“It might be my fault, but I didn’t think that kid should sit his senior year because y’all did something wrong,” Presswood said. “It was his senior year. His living situation got messed up, and he had to move with his father.”</p><p>Little Village has seven players back from last season, but Presswood is no longer the coach. He resigned to care for his elderly parents.</p><p>The IHSA website doesn’t currently list a boys basketball coach for Little Village. Sharena Atkinson, Little Village's athletic director, did not respond to a request for comment on this story or the open basketball coaching position.</p><p>“It just sits with me knowing we did the work and still didn’t get the opportunity,” Boyd said. “Basketball has been one of the main focuses all my high school years, and this was the goal I kept pushing for. Losing it like this is tough.”<br></p>
