entries.title: Former Bears Pro Bowl returner Cordarrelle Patterson arrested
entries.summary: <p>Cordarrelle Patterson, who went to two Pro Bowls as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> kickoff returner in 2019 and 2020, was arrested Saturday on suspicion of domestic assault. He was released from the Sevier County (Tenn.) Jail later that night.<br>`<br>TMZ reported Tuesday that Patterson's wife accused him of grabbing her by her upper hair and her hair.</p><p>Patterson played in the NFL from 2013-24, going to two Pro Bowls each with the Vikings and Bears. Patterson also played for the Raiders, Patriots, Falcons and, in 2024, the Steelers. He was used as both a receiver and running back. In his career, Patterson returned nine kickoffs for touchdowns, the most in the history of the NFL. He had one kickoff return touchdown in 2019 and another in 2020 for the Bears and was named a first-team all-pro both years.</p><p>Patterson attended the University of Tennessee, about an hour from his current home.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Oficial fuera de servicio acusado de disparar dos armas en La Villita pierde sus poderes policiales
entries.summary: <p>A un policía de Chicago le retiraron sus facultades policiales luego de que funcionarios de supervisión informaran que había disparado con dos armas durante un tiroteo mientras se encontraba fuera de servicio en La Villita, dejando a un hombre herido a principios de este mes.</p><p>El oficial Edgar Delgado Arroyo fue relevado de sus funciones el martes, dijo un portavoz policial. Ahora está asignado a la Sección de Respuesta Alterna, una unidad integrada por policías con problemas disciplinarios y otros que no están médicamente aptos para el servicio completo.</p><p>La Oficina Civil de Responsabilidad Policial (COPA) dijo que el oficial fuera de servicio conducía por la cuadra 2600 al oeste de 26th Street la madrugada del 4 de octubre cuando se encontró con un grupo de personas, tuvo una discusión y abrió fuego.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9f0000" name="module-9f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Luego condujo hacia la cuadra 2300 al sur de Rockwell Street y “disparó tiros adicionales con dos armas simultáneamente”, en dirección del encuentro inicial, dijo COPA.</p><p>Un hombre fue alcanzado dos veces y fue llevado al hospital Mount Sinai en condición estable, según la policía.</p><p>Una fuente policial dijo que Delgado Arroyo se dirigió a la zona después de que su madre reportara que disparos anteriores habían impactado su casa. La fuente agregó que su padre había sido asesinado en un tiroteo cercano en julio de 2021.</p><p>Según la fuente, el oficial hablaba por teléfono con el 911 cuando fue impactado y posteriormente abrió fuego; la fuente describió a la víctima por disparos como un hombre de 24 años vinculado a la pandilla Satan's Disciples.</p><p>La policía investiga si hubo un intercambio de disparos después de que Delgado Arroyo abrió fuego inicialmente, dijo la fuente.</p><p>Delgado Arroyo no respondió a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>Líderes comunitarios han planteado dudas sobre el tiroteo y han exigido que se presenten cargos contra el oficial.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Man sought in 2021 killing of National Guard member added to FBI's 10 most wanted list
entries.summary: <p>The FBI on Tuesday added a man <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/06/07/racketeering-indictment-national-guard-soldier-chrys-carvajal" target="_blank" >accused in the 2021 murder</a> of Illinois National Guard soldier Chrys Carvajal to its "Ten Most Wanted Fugitives"<b> </b>list, increasing the reward for the man's capture to $1 million.</p><p>The feds are looking for Joseph<b> </b>"Troubles"<b> </b>Matos, 44, a purported member of the Milwaukee Kings street gang. Matos has ties to Dallas and California but is believed to be hiding in the Chicago area, authorities said. </p><p>"Today's addition of Matos to the FBI's notorious Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list ensures that his face and description will be found on every FBI-affiliated website and social media platform, and this case will now be on every phone around the world until he is apprehended," said Ryan<b> </b>Whalen, the special agent in charge of the FBI's Chicago Field Office.</p><p>Matos is 6'2", weighs 220 pounds and has brown hair and eyes. His tattoos include the words "M-Town Kings" on the right side of his neck, "1300" on the left side of his neck, "Move in Silence" on his right hand, "Trust no one" on his left hand and "Heavensent, Hellbound" on his arms, according to the FBI.</p><p>Tattooed on his belly are the words "MOST WANTED,"<b> </b>authorities said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: 200 live cockroaches, 'black slime' found at Lake View hospital cafeteria during failed inspection
entries.summary: <p>Alternative meal arrangements have been set up at the cafeteria at Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center in Lake View after it failed a health inspection Friday in which "black slime" and more than 200 live cockroaches were found in multiple food preparation areas.</p><p>The cockroaches were found near the grill, fryer, steamer and storage areas of the cafeteria at the medical center, 836 W. Wellington Ave., according to Chicago Department of Public Health records. </p><p>Additionally, black slime also built up on an ice machine and dripped onto ice cubes that were used for human consumption, the records show. </p><p>In a statement, the medical center said they were arranging alternative meal services. </p><p>“We recognize the importance of maintaining the highest standards for food safety and are taking the necessary steps to address the findings and meet all requirements to safely resume kitchen operations," the medical center said in the statement. "In the meantime, patients continue to receive meals without interruption, with alternative food preparation and meal service arrangements in place.” </p><p>The public health department has not responded to requests for comment.<br></p>

entries.title: La policía busca a tres sospechosos que agredieron a un hombre de 65 años en la Línea Roja
entries.summary: <p>La Policía de Chicago busca a tres personas que golpearon a un hombre mayor y luego lo arrastraron de un tren de la Línea Roja de la CTA el 9 de octubre.</p><p>El hombre, de 65 años, viajaba en el tren en la cuadra 1200 al norte de Clark Street, cerca de la estación Clark/Division de la Línea Roja, cuando los tres lo golpearon y lo arrastraron fuera del tren y luego le pintaron la cara con pintura en aerosol, dijo la policía.</p><p>Los sospechosos fueron descritos como un hombre de unos 20 años con el pelo estilo “shag” y el número 5718 tatuado en los nudillos de la mano izquierda.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7f0000" name="module-7f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El otro agresor, también de unos 20 años, vestía un suéter oscuro, pantalones color beige y llevaba aretes. Iban acompañados por una mujer de unos 20 años que vestía un abrigo color café, pantalones negros y botas cafés, dijo la policía.</p><p>Cualquier persona que tenga información puede comunicarse con los detectives al 312-745-4447.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Five beluga whales have died at Shedd since Aug. 25, but CEO Bridget Coughlin says this is no crisis
entries.summary: <p>On a recent morning, Shedd Aquarium President and CEO Bridget Coughlin stood in front of a pool filled with six frolicking beluga whales, insisting that the institution, where five other whales have died in recent weeks, is not in crisis.</p><p>Coughlin, who has a doctorate in biochemistry, also pushed back against a growing public perception that the aquarium might have bitten off more than it could chew in adding 10 more belugas to a population of eight resident whales.</p><p>“Rescue is never convenient,” Coughlin said. “We have been truly rescuing these animals since January, when we sent the first staff up to Marineland [Canada in Ontario] to observe the animals, talk with Marineland staff, look at their records, watch their social groupings. So while to many it might have seemed recent, this has been a really diligent, multi-step process.”</p><p>Five aquariums, including four in the United States, agreed to take Marineland’s 30 belugas (at the time, the world largest population of captive belugas), after the park threatened to euthanize the cetaceans, saying the facility had run out of money to care for them. To date, six Marineland belugas have died since being moved: four at Shedd and one each at SeaWorld San Diego and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain. (A fifth Shedd beluga, Beethoven, was a resident whale and died Sept. 2.)</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Much of the criticism for the transport out of Marineland has come from animal rights activists, who called the Canadian aquatic park’s threat to kill the belugas a “manufactured crisis” that effectively forced the Canadian government to approve shipping out the whales.</p><p>Largely forgotten in the drama of moving the whales — first in trucks and then in the cargo hold of a Boeing 777 — were the people left behind: the Marineland trainers. Because the park was sometimes understaffed, shifts often lasted 12 hours. The bond between animal and human became incredibly close, former staff there say, making the threat of euthanasia, the transports out and the eventual death of some whales deeply traumatizing.</p><p>Alysha Tullio, who lives in Ontario, spent four years working at Marineland, starting as a basic beluga caregiver, before becoming the lead trainer for two of the belugas that ended up at Shedd, including Sierra.</p><p>Tullio remembers the day Sierra was hoisted out of her pool at Marineland and loaded into a truck.</p><p>“I patted her on her melon, said, ‘I love you,’ and hoped she’d be okay,” Tullio said.</p><p>Tullio was close too with Rain and Caspian, two whales that later died at Shedd: Rain, a 20-year-old female, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/09/03/shedd-aquarium-beluga" target="_blank" ><u>died Sept. 2</u></a>; Caspian, 27, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/09/5th-beluga-whale-dies-at-shedd-aquarium" target="_blank" ><u>died Oct. 7</u></a>. The two other belugas to die were Peekachu, a 23-year-old female, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/26/one-of-the-shedds-rescued-beluga-whales-has-died" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>And in a followup email in response to Tullio’s concerns, Shedd spokesman Johnny Ford noted that the Chicago institution spent seven months before the rescue in close collaboration with Marineland veterinarians and animal care staff. Ford said that that collaboration continued after the whales arrived at Shedd.</p><p>“When we needed to share news of the losses, we first contacted Marineland’s supervisors,” Ford said. “We knew this would be painful news for the people who had cared for these whales, and we wanted to give their former staff the time and consideration they deserved. We expected the supervisors to connect with those team members directly and share the news.”</p><p>Some animal rights activists say the beluga deaths point to a bigger issue: the need to put an end to breeding whales in captivity and, by doing so, slowly phase out whales housed in tanks.</p><p>“Personally, I want to focus on these six animals swimming behind us and doing right by them. … ,” Coughlin said. “Animal welfare is a science-based question. So I can’t predict the science in the future for what is best for these animals. What I want to do right now is to make sure we get Sierra her eyedrops, Secord eating a more robust diet. Let’s take care of these animals now and evaluate the science ongoing for the future.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Hombre que provocó cierre de la corte federal de Chicago se declara culpable, enfrenta dos años de prisión
entries.summary: <p>El hombre que provocó el cierre, la evacuación y un enfrentamiento que duró horas en la Corte Federal Dirksen el año pasado se declaró culpable el jueves de poseer un arma peligrosa en una instalación de la corte federal y ahora enfrenta hasta dos años de prisión.</p><p>La jueza federal Mary Rowland fijó la fecha de sentencia de Mario Santoyo para el 12 de enero. Santoyo admitió ante la jueza que había llevado un cuchillo con una navaja de más de 2½ pulgadas al edificio en julio de 2025.</p><p>Cuando un fiscal relató brevemente las acusaciones contra Santoyo, Rowland preguntó si eran exactas.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-040000" name="module-040000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Eso es factual”, le dijo Santoyo a la jueza.</p><p>Santoyo, de 40 años, también llevaba una mochila el día del cierre del juzgado. Las autoridades “no tenían idea” de lo que había dentro, reconoció su abogado.</p><p>El enfrentamiento resultante duró aproximadamente nueve horas, paralizó el tráfico en la calle Dearborn y ultimadamente provocó la evacuación de la torre de 30 pisos en el centro de la ciudad.</p><p>Aunque Santoyo se declaró culpable de un delito que conlleva una pena máxima de dos años de prisión, las directrices federales señalan una condena de no más de seis meses tras las rejas, estimaron las autoridades el jueves.</p><p>Cuando Santoyo llegó a la corte ubicada en 219 S. Dearborn alrededor de las 10:30 a.m. el 22 de julio de 2025, mandó llamar al FBI y afirmó que “gangsters” o "gangbangers" (pandilleros) estaban tratando de matarlo, según una denuncia penal.</p><p>Después de que un oficial de seguridad de la corte le dijera que las oficinas del FBI estaban en otro lugar y le pidiera que se marchara, Santoyo sacó un cuchillo, se lo acercó a su propio cuello y dijo que se iba a hacer daño, muestran los registros.</p><p>Los ocupantes del edificio en los pisos superiores fueron notificados por bocina sobre el incidente y se les dijo que evitaran el vestíbulo. Las autoridades despejaron Federal Plaza y el otro lado de la calle, el tráfico en Dearborn dejó de fluir y un dron comenzó a sobrevolar cerca de la entrada de la corte.</p><p>Más tarde, alrededor de las 2 p.m., los funcionarios judiciales les indicaron a las personas en la cafetería del segundo piso cómo salir del edificio de forma segura. Poco después, declararon la evacuación obligatoria. Los funcionarios guiaron a la gente por las salidas en el lado este del vestíbulo y luego hacia State Street.</p><p>También se pudo ver a agentes de la ley registrando un Chevrolet Impala plateado estacionado cerca de Jackson Street y Dearborn.</p><p>No fue hasta cerca de las 8 p.m. que las fuerzas del orden “usaron fuerza no letal” y detuvieron a Santoyo, muestran los registros. Soltó el cuchillo que tenía pero resultó que llevaba una segunda navaja, según los federales.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: CTA wants your feedback to improve bus service
entries.summary: <p>Got an idea to improve CTA bus service? The agency wants your input.</p><p>The survey is available online at <a class="Link" href="https://ctabusvisionproject.com/" target="_blank" >CTABusVisionProject.com</a> until Nov. 30.</p><p>The CTA is looking for ways to increase bus speeds and improve transfers with Metra and Pace.</p><p>The agency says it is considering these changes:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-abfc2a22-ccb6-11f1-8ee1-bf75a5a30ec2"><li>increased frequency</li><li>expanded service hours</li><li>route adjustments</li><li>enhanced transfers and connections</li><li>and "new bus priority infrastructure"</li></ul><p>The survey takes around 20 minutes. Participants will be entered into a lottery for one of five $100 digital Visa gift cards.</p><p>The CTA will also take feedback during 10 in-person community events though the end of November. A full list of them is available on the survey website.</p><p>The CTA plans to submit the input to its oversight agency, the Northern Illinois Transit Authority, at the end of the year. NITA takes over service planning for CTA, Metra and Pace in 2027.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/10/12/nita-dream-transit-project-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >We asked for your dream transit project. Here’s what you told us.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: After years of false hope, Bulls pick Caleb Wilson feels inevitable
entries.summary: <p>There’s been hope surrounding previous <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> draft picks the last 18 years.</p><p>Plenty of hope.</p><p>Hope that Doug McDermott was worth trading for with Denver in 2014, hope that Bobby Portis could turn into the next Joakim Noah a year later. Heck, there was even initial excitement around Denzel Valentine when he was grabbed at No. 14 in the 2016 June draft and a month later the Michigan State standout was hitting a game-winner in the Summer League Championship game.</p><p>Wendell Carter, Chandler Hutchison, Patrick Williams selected No. 4 overall in 2020 … hope, hope, hope.</p><p>The organization became experts in building it on draft night and the Bulls fans became well-versed in slurping it up.</p><p>Sometimes the gut-punch was immediate, like when it was obvious that Marquis Teague (2012) was not a legit NBA player just a few months into his rookie year. Other times it was a slow burn, like the former front office continuing to remind everyone of the fact that Williams was only 18, then 19, then he was only 20.</p><p>Be patient.</p><p>That’s why the Caleb Wilson experience feels different.</p><p>Sure, there’s hope surrounding the rookie out of North Carolina, but there’s also building momentum of certainty. A certainty not felt since Derrick Rose was selected No. 1 overall 18 years ago.</p><p>And it’s not just local hype or Bulls messaging, either. It’s nationally, other executives, other NBA coaches acknowledging that Wilson’s rise to stardom feels inevitable.</p><p>That’s why all eyes will be on the Bulls Wednesday night in Toronto, as Wilson and his teammates tip-off the 2026-27 regular-season campaign.</p><p>“I’m just really excited for the opportunity to play,” Wilson said of his pending real-game debut. “I mean I’ve been waiting on this opportunity my whole life and it’s finally here, so just really a lot of excitement.”</p><p>Bulls fans have been waiting almost just as long for a player like this.</p><p>And the good news seen throughout the summer, into training camp, and then the preseason games? Wilson not only talks about chasing down greatness but embraces the work it takes to chase that down and does so with a work ethic not seen by many 20-year-olds.</p><p>His new executive vice president of basketball operations in Bryson Graham has seen that for months.</p><p>Graham detailed his own day-to-day since drafting Wilson and admitted anytime he’s been in the Advocate Center at night he can hear a bouncing ball and music. Two sure signs that it’s Wilson getting in extra shots.</p><p>For Wilson, however, it’s just what you do in pursuit of lofty goals.</p><p>“I feel like I’m prepared for the moment and the opportunity,” Wilson said. “It’s just a matter of going out there and show what I can do.”</p><p>Not the only player offering up hope to this fan base, either.</p><p>While Wilson feels like the headliner, Matas Buzelis has a chance to be one heck of an opening act, entering Year 3 in what could be a breakout season.</p><p>There’s a real possibility that the Bulls are a mere 30-win team, but if Buzelis and Wilson prove to be a one-two punch that averages 20 and 10 and look like foundation pieces for this rebuild, pack up the gear in mid-April and call it a very successful season.</p><p>Step 1 comes against the Raptors, however, and does so even with coach Tiago Splitter trying to calm the hype.</p><p>“Caleb has a tower of things on his mind right now, you know,” Splitter said. “Like first NBA game, how we play on offense, how we play on defense, there’s a lot of things going on, and sometimes you just got to relax a little bit and just go out and hoop. Slowly he’ll get those things better. I just want to see them enjoying and competing every night, and that’s all I can ask.”</p>

entries.title: Comienza la votación temprana en todos los 50 distritos políticos de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Richard Rolark quería evitar las filas, las molestias y la posibilidad de que haya mal tiempo el día de las elecciones dentro de dos semanas.</p><p>“Es una buena comodidad para la gente mayor, especialmente aquí en el lado sur. Y el 3 de noviembre no sabes cómo estará el clima. Esto es Chicago, después de todo. Podríamos tener 8 pulgadas de nieve y 40 grados bajo cero”, dijo Rolark, de 76 años, el lunes por la mañana afuera del sitio de votación del distrito 4 en el Centro de Servicios Comunitarios Dr. Martin Luther King.</p><p>La votación anticipada presencial ampliada para las elecciones generales del 3 de noviembre <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/news/expanded-person-early-voting-opens-today-all-50-chicago-wards-november-3rd-general-election" target="_blank" >comenzó el lunes en los 50 distritos de Chicago</a> y en tres universidades del área de Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-920000" name="module-920000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En la ciudad, los votantes elegirán al presidente y a los miembros de la Junta de Educación de Chicago. A nivel estatal, los votantes emitirán su voto en las contiendas para el Senado de Estados Unidos, la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos, la gobernación y la vicegobernación de Illinois, así como para fiscal general, otros cargos estatales y sus representantes locales en la Asamblea General de Illinois.</p><p>Rolark, veterano de Vietnam y residente del vecindario de Bronzeville, dijo que cree que la gente no debe de dar por hecho su derecho al voto.</p><p>“Salgan a votar. Eso es algo muy, muy importante. Yo solía marchar con el Dr. King para conseguir el derecho al voto”, dijo Rolark.</p><p>Rolark contó que en 1965, con 15 años, estaba marchando en Selma, Alabama, con otros activistas por los derechos de voto cuando fueron atacados por policías estatales en el puente Edmund Pettus.</p><p>“Nunca llegué a cruzar el puente. Era muy joven. Nos subieron al autobús cuando empezaron a tirar piedras. Me golpearon con una piedra. Fue una experiencia que nunca voy a olvidar”, dijo Rolark. “Les digo a las personas que voten y me dicen ‘no me va a servir de nada. No necesito votar’. Me golpearon en la parte de atrás de la cabeza con una piedra por intentar conseguir el derecho al voto. No me digan que no vote. Es tu derecho.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f59028" name="image-f59028"></a> entries.title: Previewing and predicting the 2026 IHSA Class 7A state football playoffs
entries.summary: <p>Playing East St. Louis is such a frightening prospect for most high school football programs that some area teams moved up to Class 7A, likely to avoid the Flyers, who were expected to play in Class 6A.</p><p>Well, bad news for them. East St. Louis also petitioned up to Class 7A this season. The Flyers have nearly as many future college players as Mount Carmel and beat the Caravan at ISU in Week 1.</p><p>That was a statement win for East St. Louis, which Fenwick upset in the 6A title game last season.</p><p>“It means something,” Flyers coach Darren Sunkett said after beating Mount Carmel. “We had something to prove. We have been at state seven years in a row. Win or lose, we were there. It is tough to win in the state of Illinois. We came out with a chip on our shoulder. We wanted to show that we could play with Mount Carmel and beat them.”</p><p>East St. Louis has a smooth path to the semifinals. Brother Rice could be waiting. The Crusaders also beat Mount Carmel this season and won Class 7A last year.</p><p>Brother Rice has an extremely difficult road through the bracket. The Crusaders don’t have any easy wins. St. Charles North, Brother Rice’s potential First Round opponent, is a quality team. And then Batavia and undefeated Normal could be waiting before the Flyers.</p><p>The Second Round may feature some of the season's most exciting games, with Brother Rice vs. Batavia, Hersey vs. entries.title: Bears predictions: Week 7 vs. Patriots
entries.summary: <p> The Sun-Times' experts make their picks for the "Thursday Night Football" game <a class="Link" href=" https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >against the Patriots</a>: </p><h3>Patrick Finley</h3><p><b>Bears, 27-21:</b> The last time the Bears played on "TNF," they lost 6-3 to the 2024 Seahawks. Thomas Brown was the interim head coach. Caleb Williams had a 53 passer rating and was sacked seven times. <b>Season</b>: 2-4.</p><h3>Jason Lieser</h3><p><b>Bears, 24-23</b>: The battle of the two best quarterbacks of the 2024 draft class comes down to the final seconds and a pressure-packed field-goal kick for Cairo Santos. <b>Season:</b> 3-3.</p><h3>Scoop Jackson</h3><p><b>Bears, 28-24 : </b>Sometimes football can be a game of match-ups. Williams vs. Drake Maye. Bears' injury-riddled defensive line vs. Pats' injury-riddled offensive line. CB Kyler Gordon vs. CBs Christian Gonzalez and Charles Woods. This won’t be your grandaddy’s Super Bowl XX rematch. <b>Season</b>: 2-4.</p><h3>Steve Greenberg</h3><p><b>Bears, 23-17: </b>The Patriots are so banged-up on the offensive line, their next move is seeing if Hall of Famer John Hannah wants to come out of retirement. In terms of injuries, this just plain is a worse time for the AFC champs to have to deal with such a quick turnaround than it is for the Bears. <b>Season</b>: 4-2.</p><h3>Jeff Agrest</h3><p><b>Bears, 35-19:</b> Remember the last time the Patriots visited Soldier Field? During Williams’ rookie season, the Bears totaled 142 yards in a horrendous 19-3 loss, the third of what would be 10 consecutive defeats. That’s how bad things were. This is how good things are. <b>Season</b>: 2-4.</p>

entries.title: Thieves crash Jeep into Uptown gas station, steal ATM
entries.summary: <p>A group of four burglars crashed a Jeep into an Uptown gas station and took an ATM early Tuesday on the North Side. </p><p>Officers responded to a traffic crash just after 3 a.m. in the 5100 block of North Broadway and found that a blue Jeep had crashed into the gas station, according to Chicago police. </p><p>A witness told officers three people in a black SUV entered the gas station through the hole made by the Jeep and took an ATM, police said. </p><p>The burglars then put the ATM in the SUV before fleeing in the SUV with the driver of the Jeep, officials said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Mayor Johnson budget seeks to reopen city mental health clinic next year
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s 2027 budget proposes using city funds to reopen a community mental health clinic and create permanent funding for the Crisis Assistance Response and Engagement program.</p><p>Johnson plans to announce the city’s investments in mental health services Wednesday during the unveiling of his 2027 budget. The investment will include $5 million to make <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/02/mental-health-response-teams-now-have-night-time-hours-city-officials-say" target="_blank" ><u>CARE</u></a>, which dispatches a mental health team to certain 911 calls, a permanent city program, Johnson said.</p><p>“I’ve made a commitment to ensure that people can receive treatment that they need, and this is a direct investment to bolster our work around community safety,” Johnson said in an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times/WBEZ this week.</p><p>He said the investment to reopen another mental health clinic is part of his promise to reverse the city’s past actions of shuttering community clinics. Between 1989 and 2012, the city closed 14 mental health clinics, leaving only five in place by 2016, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://igchicago.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/OIG-Audit-of-CDPHs-Mental-Equity-Program.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>2025 audit</u></a> of the city’s mental health equity initiative. Johnson did not provide specifics about where the mental health clinic would open in 2027 or how much it could cost.</p><p>He plans to lean on funds allocated to the groundbreaking and controversial <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/21/brandon-johnson-social-media-tax-chicago-budget" target="_blank" ><u>social media tax</u></a>, which collects 50 cents per Chicago user after the first 100,000 users.</p><p>The city has collected more funds than anticipated from social media companies, and it's on pace to collect<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/15/brandon-johnson-social-media-tax-windfall-meta-facebook-instagram-tiktok-linkedin" target="_blank" ><u> $49.2 million</u></a> by the end of the year. But those funds are being held in escrow pending litigation on the tax. Still, Johnson said he’s confident the city will prevail in court, especially since the state has since enacted a similar tax.</p><p>“We’re pretty confident about our ability to move through the litigation process and have the permanent revenue stream to make sure that we’re protecting our public institutions, and especially mental and behavioral healthcare,” Johnson said.</p><p>In recent years, Johnson’s administration reopened city-run mental health clinics in Pilsen and Roseland. In 2025, the city’s budget allocated about $12.2 million for mental health clinics. The city’s larger budget for mental health programming in recent years has leaned heavily on federal funds from the American Rescue Plan Act, according to the 2025 audit.</p><p>Johnson’s 2027 budget proposal calls for $5 million for CARE, which is similar to the federal funds allocated for it. About $5.2 million in funds from the American Rescue Plan was allocated for the program, but those federal funds end this year.</p><p>“The motivation for me has always been based upon just lived experiences, and the fact that, you know, you had previous administrations that actually shut down mental and behavioral healthcare, right?” Johnson said. “And previous administrations that refused to make these investments. So my motivation is certainly very much connected to the need that is substantial.”</p><p>The federal funds were used to staff citywide operations. The teams respond to requests for mental health services via 911 calls or when a dispatcher initiates a CARE response. The program recently expanded its hours from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., the city previously announced.</p><p>Johnson said the city continues to work on building trust for these new services, pointing to an increase in calls for CARE teams.</p><p>“The more we make this readily available, I believe that that confidence will continue to grow,” Johnson said.</p>
entries.author: Elvia Malagón

entries.title: Evanston students say some New Trier fans spat on them, used racist, homophobic slurs at NU's Ryan Field
entries.summary: <p>It should have been a landmark night for football, with Evanston and New Trier, rivals for more than a century, facing off before a crowd of about 25,000 people at Northwestern's new Ryan Field.</p><p>Instead, members of the Evanston Township High School marching band say the evening was marred by racist and homophobic slurs and taunts hurled at them by New Trier Township High School students.</p><p>The ETHS students said they were booed and yelled at before and after the game, with some told to “go back to Africa,” and “kill yourself.” Adri Lieberman, 17, a color guard captain, said she comforted two of her friends after they were spat on by New Trier students.</p><p>“When I got back to the band room, I just see them both walk in, sobbing, and my first instinct was to hug them and just hold them,” Lieberman said. “It just really tore at me and it made me really upset.”</p><p>Kaleem Alam, 16, said they felt “degraded” when they heard students yelling racial slurs, including the n-word. </p><p>“Behind that word it’s like centuries of slavery happening,” Alam said. </p><p>The New Trier crowd, they added, was mostly made up of white students. At New Trier's Winnetka campus, which serves grades 10 through 12, about 73% of students are white, according to 2025 data from the Illinois Report Card, compared to ETHS, where 44% of students in grades 9 through 12 are white.</p><p>Ifeoluwa Dada, 16, said she and her friends were stunned by the online response they saw after details of what happened became public. She said some commenters told ETHS students to “get thicker skin" and that they "probably deserved it."</p><p>The Sun-Times reviewed screenshots shared by Dada showing those comments. The Sun-Times also found several social media commenters questioning students’ version of events, demanding audio or video proof and characterizing the behavior as “normal.” </p><p>Many comments on TikTok and Instagram reels posted by news outlets also invoked the longstanding rivalry between the two schools. Some commenters who identified themselves as alumni said similar incidents had occurred between the rival schools for decades.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cc0000" name="image-cc0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/42c9120/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F0f%2F7f5913ae443f82220eccc2c05c62%2Fmarchingband-261021-05.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/421f06f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F0f%2F7f5913ae443f82220eccc2c05c62%2Fmarchingband-261021-05.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/015d087/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F0f%2F7f5913ae443f82220eccc2c05c62%2Fmarchingband-261021-05.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Evanston Township High School marching band members (from left): Ifeoluwa Dada, 16, a junior, Adri Lieberman, 17, a senior, and Kaleem Alam, 16, a junior, photographed in the band room at the high school on Monday, October 19, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/015d087/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F0f%2F7f5913ae443f82220eccc2c05c62%2Fmarchingband-261021-05.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c2840e1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F0f%2F7f5913ae443f82220eccc2c05c62%2Fmarchingband-261021-05.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/015d087/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F0f%2F7f5913ae443f82220eccc2c05c62%2Fmarchingband-261021-05.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Evanston Township High School marching band members (from left) Ifeoluwa Dada, 16, a junior, Adri Lieberman, 17, a senior, and Kaleem Alam, 16, a junior, said members of the band were subjected to racial and homophobic slurs at Friday night’s football game against New Trier at the new Ryan Field. They discussed what happened after a concert on Monday at the high school. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Octavio Jones/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dada said New Trier cheerleaders intentionally bumped into Evanston band members during tailgating before the game.</p><p>Evanston students want meaningful consequences for New Trier, she said.</p><p>“I just want them to know, if they do this, then there has to be something done, and that something is either suspension or getting banned from Ryan Field,” Dada said.</p><p>Administrators from both districts have announced they’re investigating the incident. They released a joint statement on Sunday. </p><p>“Friday evening should have been an opportunity to celebrate our students, spirited competition, and the longstanding traditions of our two school communities,” the statement said. “For the ETHS Marching Band, it was an especially meaningful opportunity to do what they love: share their talents and proudly represent their school. No student should leave an event where they came to perform, compete, or support their peers feeling that their dignity or belonging were demeaned.”</p><p>In an email to the Sun-Times, New Trier's chief communications officer Niki Dizon said the investigation was ongoing and that the school had no additional updates to share. She reiterated that the school does not tolerate racism, homophobia or other forms of discrimination at school or school events, and it would take appropriate action as the investigation progresses. </p><p>Illinois High School Association Executive Director Craig Anderson also has issued a statement, saying, in part: "It is sad and unfortunate that such a historic night celebrating the power of community and high school sports was marred by the despicable actions of a few." Anderson also noted both schools are working together to identify those involved, including to verify if they are current high school students and if they attend either school. </p><p>At Monday’s New Trier school board meeting, Board President Sally Tomlinson said any behavior contradicting the district’s values of inclusion and belonging must be “unequivocally condemned and addressed.” She said the district had a responsibility to strengthen inclusive and supportive spaces even if the students involved in the alleged behavior are not identified.</p><p>Lieberman used to live in Wilmette, and noted she would have attended New Trier had she not moved to Evanston before starting high school.</p><p>“It’s an event like this that makes me really proud to be an Evanston [student] and not a New Trier student," she said, "because I think about this and I’m just like, ‘This is really disgusting and really horrible."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Mayor Johnson wants to pour $24 million into city's summer youth jobs program
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is pitching a $24 million increase to the city’s summer youth jobs program that would fund 7,000 more positions in 2027.</p><p>The increase would bring the total number of jobs to roughly 40,000 by next year, bringing to full fruition one of Johnson’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2023/4/21/23693330/mayor-elect-brandon-johnson-double-summer-jobs-chicagos-teens-youth-violence" target="_blank" ><u>cornerstone campaign promises</u></a> to double the city’s youth employment program.</p><p>Johnson told WBEZ it is “one of the most consequential” proposals in his 2027 spending plan.</p><p>“I made a commitment to increase the number of opportunities for young people to have paid jobs throughout the summer, and this is going to put us that much closer to meeting the overwhelming demand that young people have in terms of wanting jobs,” Johnson said.</p><p>The city’s summer jobs program, now known as Chicago Youth Works, started under former Mayor Rahm Emanuel. The city hires young people directly at its sister agencies, like the Chicago Park District, doles out grants to community organizations, and partners with corporations, like the Chicago Bulls, to hire kids.</p><p>Kids work as restaurant servers, retail workers, yoga studio staffers, grocery store stockers, in government offices and more. The employment program runs for a limited time frame over the summer: just six weeks.</p><p>The number of applicants has consistently outpaced the number of jobs available for young people between the ages of 14 and 24, with nearly 60,000 kids applying for jobs each year. And a recent survey of Chicago teens by the group My Block. My Hood. My City. showed <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/moment-of-youth/2026/09/25/downtown-day-teen-survey-results" target="_blank" ><u>kids are craving jobs and businesses</u></a> in their South and West Side neighborhoods.</p><p>The summer before Johnson took office, the city funded 20,544 positions, still suffering from a big pandemic-era dip. The year before the pandemic, the city funded 31,552 youth positions.</p><p>Johnson has steadily <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/07/09/chicagos-summer-jobs-program-sees-another-year-of-growth-following-pandemic-era-dip" target="_blank" ><u>boosted the number of jobs</u></a> annually during his freshman tenure, marking one of his most tangible campaign promises kept. Johnson increased funding for youth employment by $6.2 million this year, and by $25.6 million in 2025, according to the city’s budget office.</p><p>“I've been very much motivated to ensure that young people in this city have those opportunities and that we fund them because it's not just creating life skills — it's saving lives,” Johnson said.</p><p>Johnson’s office said that the city has seen declines in violent crime over the summer in the five community areas where the greatest number of participants were hired this year — Austin, Auburn Gresham, Roseland, South Shore and North Lawndale. Auburn Gresham, though, has seen a 14% increase in homicides from this year compared to last.</p><p>Johnson’s plans to increase youth hiring could get stuck in the cross hairs of what’s sure to be a contentious budget battle with the City Council caucus that took control of the 2026 budget process.</p><p>The city is facing, and must close, a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2026/09/03/mayor-brandon-johnson-2027-budget-forecast-chicago-city-hall-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>$882.4 million budget gap for 2027</u></a>, with limited authority to raise new types of revenue.</p><p>Johnson’s pitch to close that gap, in part, is through <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/20/mayor-brandon-johnson-failed-corporate-head-tax-resurrected-proposed-budget" target="_blank" ><u>a new corporate head tax</u></a> that would apply a $25 per-employee tax on companies with 125 or more workers. It would rake in $101 million a year, the budget office estimates.</p><p>But Johnson’s Council opposition of mostly moderate and conservative alders, who killed a similar head tax proposal of his last year, have all but called that idea dead on arrival, deeming it a “job killer.”</p><p>When asked whether he would be willing to negotiate on the size of the increase he’s pitching to the summer jobs program as part of the budget process, Johnson avoided the question and pointed back to the value he sees in the program.</p><p>“It is proven that violence amongst young people is reduced as a result of these investments,” he reiterated.</p>
entries.author: Mariah Woelfel

entries.title: Scandal, early-season struggles behind him, Mike Vrabel has the Patriots back on track for Super Bowl run
entries.summary: <p>Patriots coach Mike Vrabel took questions from the Boston-area media for 14 minutes Tuesday, lingering long enough to call on one reporter who apparently didn’t even have one, and the name Dianna Russini never came up.</p><p>Everything is mostly back to normal for Vrabel after weathering the offseason scandal of his personal relationship with Russini — a former national NFL reporter — and the Patriots stumbling out of the gate with two losses in their first three games. That’s unlikely to get more than a passing mention, if it comes up at all, on the broadcast when the Bears host the Patriots on Thursday.</p><p>Instead, the focus will be on the Patriots having won three games in a row and chasing a repeat trip to the Super Bowl, as well as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> shooting for the same destination now that starting quarterback Caleb Williams is back.</p><p>Winning covers up all sorts of issues, and Vrabel always has been a winner. After winning three Super Bowls with the Patriots as a player, he had a winning record and three playoff appearances as the Titans’ coach. That’s why the Bears were interested in him after firing Matt Eberflus in 2025.</p><p>Vrabel was, in fact, the first candidate they interviewed for the vacancy, and they spoke with Ben Johnson a few days later. One day after Johnson interviewed with the Bears, Vrabel accepted the Patriots’ job.</p><p>The two took on nearly identical rebuilds, and Vrabel has the early lead in the race to take their teams to the top. Johnson’s first season with the Bears was terrific, with the team improving by six victories and winning its first playoff game in 15 years. But Vrabel trumped it by taking the Patriots from 4-13 to 13-4 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/04/from-vastly-different-backgrounds-super-bowl-coaches-mike-vrabel-mike-macdonald-strike-perfect-tone" target="_blank" >and a spot in the Super Bowl</a>.</p><p>Each inherited a promising quarterback coming off a choppy rookie season, too. The Patriots’ Drake Maye was the No. 3 pick in the 2024 draft, two spots behind Williams. Both made major strides under their new coaches, and Maye led the NFL with a 113.5 passer rating last season en route to finishing as the runner-up in MVP voting.</p><p>Vrabel won Coach of the Year, and Johnson finished fourth. He also won the award in 2021 with the Titans, and Johnson shouted out Vrabel’s résumé unprompted at his news conference Tuesday.</p><p>They’ll go head-to-head Thursday with Johnson as the play-caller of a Bears offense that ranks fifth in the NFL, despite missing Williams for half the season so far because of a hamstring injury. Vrabel has shaped a Patriots defense that was eighth last season and ranks sixth now, though defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr calls the plays.</p><p>The exposure and fallout of Vrabel’s involvement with Russini threatened to unravel everything he had built in his first season coaching the Patriots. There were calls for him to lose his job — Russini essentially lost hers — and he stepped away from the team during the draft.</p><p>When the Patriots started 1-2, the tension rose. A radio host’s assertion of friction between Vrabel and Maye got so much attention they had to address it. Maye called Vrabel ‘‘one of the best football coaches I’ve had in my life,’’ and Vrabel said, ‘‘I wanted to coach here because Drake was the quarterback.’’</p><p>Maye threw three touchdown passes in a victory against the Bills a few days later.</p><p>Everything has smoothed out now, and the Patriots are back on track. They’re the best all-around team the Bears will have played to this point. And while the Bears are absolutely happy to have Johnson, there’s no question Vrabel is among the most challenging opponents he’ll face this season.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Bears report: Guard Jonah Jackson upgraded to limited
entries.summary: <p>What happened Tuesday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >at Halas Hall</a>:</p><h3><b>Jackson getting better</b></h3><p>Guard Jonah Jackson, who has injuries to his hip and quad, was upgraded to limited in the estimated injury report Tuesday. The Bears held a walk-through but filed a report detailing who would have been able to participate in a standard practice.</p><p>If Jackson can’t play, the Bears will turn to Luke Newman, who replaced him Sunday.</p><p>Running back Kyle Monangai remains out and is unlikely to play Thursday. Linebackers T.J. Edwards (hamstring) and Jack Sanborn (concussion) wouldn’t have practiced.</p><h3><b>KB back in town</b></h3><p>The Bears will reunite with one of their best players from last season Thursday. They chose to sign safety Coby Bryant instead of re-signing Kevin Byard, who led the NFL with seven interceptions and was named a first-team All-Pro last season. He landed with the Patriots and coach Mike Vrabel, his old boss with the Titans.</p><p>‘‘I’m looking forward to going up against him,’’ wide receiver Rome Odunze said. ‘‘And hopefully after the game, after the win, I’ll say my hellos.’’</p><h3><b>Patriots guards likely out</b></h3><p>Vrabel said he doesn’t expect guards Ben Brown (knee) or Alijah Vera-Tucker to play Thursday. He said a third starting offensive lineman, tackle Morgan Moses, has a chance to come back from a foot injury in time.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Natalie Nakase learned hard work from her dad. In the WNBA playoffs, she's also had to reckon with her limits
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — It was a relief to see Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase in the press room in Chicago in late August.</p><p>I’d spent the season uncomfortable with the fact that as a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> beat reporter, I still couldn’t tell how good Tyler Marsh, the Sky's first-time coach who struggled through his first two seasons, really was.</p><p>Now here was a coach everyone agreed was great. Nakase had undeniably turned her team into something greater than the sum of its parts, ultimately leading them to the Finals in only the franchise's second year of existence.</p><p>How did she do it? From afar, Nakase gives the impression she’s outworking everyone. Maybe because of the urgency with which she stalks the sidelines, or how frequently she says the word “kill.”</p><p>But up close she conveys a certain warmth too. She’s the kind of person whose eyes light up when she sees a familiar member of the press, or when asked about a bench player’s success, or when talking about her team’s commitment to playing with joy.</p><p>I remember before the game in Chicago, the broadcaster asked her about that joy — in particular, about how it showed up on the stat sheet. Was it valuable only insofar as it led to winning, or some other measurable outcome? Nakase said no.</p><p>“There has to be some beauty in understanding that: you’re gonna lose,” she said. “You can still have joy when you’re losing. Sports has to understand that’s gonna happen.”</p><p>It felt like the soft underbelly of Nakase’s relentless aura peeking out. So I decided to find out more about the connection between the two.</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center">***</p><p>Interviewing players and coaches around the league this past week reveals that Nakase really is tough as nails. She’s obsessive about giving it her all and getting her team to “empty the tank.” That she collapsed from exhaustion during Game 3 of the quarterfinals against the Wings was the most striking and concerning example.</p><p>She said later that she’d been so excited about game planning that she’d forgotten to eat.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/GGB9Fz4fUYE?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Natalie Nakase remained coaching the rest of the game"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>As Nakase tells it, she got her work ethic from her Dad. Gary Nakase was the person who held her to the highest standard, who always put her in basketball leagues where she was the worst player so that she’d have to sink or swim.</p><p>“He’s like: ‘hey now you suck, good luck,’” she laughed.</p><p>But I did a little <a class="Link" href="https://defector.com/how-the-japanese-american-basketball-leagues-built-natalie-nakase" target="_blank" >reading</a> and found out it goes back further than that. Gary got his work ethic from his father, Kenichi, who was relocated to a Japanese internment camp during World War II, and then had to start all over.</p><p>It got me thinking about how we inherit our approaches to hard work. My grandparents, Latvian refugees from the Soviet occupation, also had to start from scratch when they came to the United States. They instilled a strong work ethic in my mom, who passed it on to me.</p><p>Over time though, I became more skeptical of the Boomers and their “just push through” attitudes toward hard work. I felt they weren’t in touch enough with their hearts or bodies to discern whether they were even working toward the right thing. I was even skeptical of my peers and the hustle culture I saw all around me — didn’t hustling so hard just release us from reckoning with our greed and cravings for prestige?</p><p>But what about when the hustlers are really trying to help people? What about someone like Nakase, who’s working toward a more noble goal?</p><p>“Coaching is never about you,” Nakase said, when asked about her purpose last week. “It should never be about you. It’s all about pouring yourself into others and building their confidence.</p><p>“And building their weaknesses into strengths and making them also understand that: it’s okay to have weaknesses.”</p><p>I had to learn that lesson about weaknesses the hard way this season.<b> </b>Six months after Nakase got her dream job with the Valkyries, I got mine covering the WNBA. That meant that for the first time in my career, I’d be contributing to a greater purpose: deepening the conversation around women’s basketball, a game I had played and coached my entire life.</p><p>Suddenly I was grinding in the ways I’d always criticized. I discovered how easy it was to fall into it. You forget to eat because the 10-hour sessions don’t even feel like work. Because you’re in flow. Because in some ways the work puts you at ease. “Film is my therapy,” Nakase said after practice last Friday.</p><p>But as anyone who’s ever been in therapy knows: it’s actually tiring as hell. It takes a toll on your body. Eventually you run into the thing that tells you you need to stop.</p><p>For me, it was muscle tension that started causing sharp pains in the back of my head. Or more accurately: it was concern from parents about the pains in the back of my head that pushed me to slow down.</p><p>I realized that to make it through the season, I had to start taking more breaks. Which, ironically, is something that my mom has encouraged me to do my whole life. I’d ignored it because I feared it wou</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d10000" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Golden State Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase speaks to the media before Game 1 of the WNBA semifinals against the Las Vegas Aces in San Francisco on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tony Avelar/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>ld be a weakness — that it cause me to fall behind.</p><p>But I discovered that not only does pausing to take a break actually improve the quality of my writing, it also helps me remember that my own purpose is not static.</p><p>My purpose on a given day might just be to breathe in and out. Or experience the pleasure of an unhurried mind. Or be available to answer the phone when a family member calls.</p><p>Sometimes I wonder if Nakase takes enough breaks to allow that kind of shift in purpose. I worry that we are the most at risk of burnout when we’re working on behalf of others, when we’re passing along virtues we learned from our parents.</p><p>So I was relieved to know that in the aftermath of Nakase’s collapse, she’s taking her family’s concerns seriously. Her sister is staying with her during the playoffs, leaving out little meals for her to eat on the go.<b> </b>She’s now wearing a heart monitor, and reflecting on how before her dad passed away in 2021, he told her to never let her career get in the way of her health.</p><p>It reminded me of my parents: the same people who taught me hard work are also trying to teach me about limits.</p><p>So before Game 1 I asked Nakase about what made her dad a cool person, mostly just to put his presence in the room. The joy lit up her face.</p><p>“What made my dad a cool person was that he was there for me every single day,” she said. “His love language was basketball, it was discipline, and it was time.”</p><p>I was struck by the word time, and realized that I’ve never really allowed myself to fully feel that gratitude to my parents — for being at every one of my games, reading every one of my articles, answering every one of my calls.</p><p>Sometimes it really does take a great coach to access a feeling that soft.</p>

entries.title: Why Blackhawks fans are frustrated by United Center parking changes, price increases this season
entries.summary: <p>Many fans drove to the United Center for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' Oct. 6 home opener and discovered — amid construction south and west of the arena — what they later described as a nightmarish parking situation.</p><p>Some fans who had purchased or received parking passes in advance for specific lots arrived at those lots, only to discover they were already full. They were then redirected by overwhelmed employees from one lot after another in search of vacancy.</p><p>Other fans waited in line to pay for drive-up parking in familiar lots, only to discover — once they reached the front of the line — those lots had been converted into pre-pay coupon-only lots. Although that had been mentioned in emails to fans, it wasn't displayed on street-side signage leading up to the lot entrances.</p><p>Many affected fans ended up missing part or all of Patrick Kane's Chicago re-introduction ceremony and the first period of the game. And after the Hawks' win, fans exiting the lots and navigating nearby streets encountered heavy congestion and ineffective traffic control.</p><p>The Hawks received many complaints, but they don't control the parking arrangement. Instead, the United Center itself does.</p><p>Fans have described a generally smoother experience for the four home games since the opener. Testimonials were largely positive this past <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/17/blackhawks-stars-connor-bedard-spencer-knight" >Saturday</a> against the Stars, for example.</p><p>But the Oct. 6 chaos has still left a bad taste in some fans' mouths — and has made others who heard about it secondhand wary of buying tickets and driving in themselves.</p><p>"[Oct. 6] was the first regular-season gameday experience for fans with an earlier start time, new traffic patterns and changes in lot assignments resulting in some arrival disruptions," a United Center spokesperson wrote to the Sun-Times.</p><p>"We have reassessed our operations and reallocated appropriate resources. We will continue to communicate updates and changes with fans."</p><p>Weeknights tend to be trickier than weekends, since some fans arrive earlier for weekend games. The Hawks' decision to move weeknight start times up 30 minutes to 7:00 p.m. — popular as it was — further condenses fans' arrival window.</p><p>So with a near-capacity crowd expected Friday against the Canadiens, those reassessments and reallocations will be put to a test again. Then on Saturday, Bulls fans will get their first tastes of the new arrangement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-credit"><p>Giacomo Cain/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Most of these United Center parking complications stem from construction, as phase one of the 1901 Project <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/03/united-center-owners-wirtz-reinsdorf-break-ground-7-billion-1901-project" >began</a> in June. A 6,000-seat music hall, 180-key hotel, retail space and two parking garages are currently being built on top of what used to be Lot K and Lot G.</p><p>That took more than 1,100 parking spots offline, requiring season-ticket members formerly assigned to those lots to be moved elsewhere.</p><p>The United Center prepared for this by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/02/24/united-center-reinsdorf-wirtz-parking-lots-arena-1901-project" >acquiring</a> a number of lots (located a few blocks east or west of the arena) that used to be privately owned, which the spokesperson said "made up for the loss of spots in K and G."</p><p>The total number of lots near the arena (regardless of ownership) has decreased nonetheless, but total capacity has never really been an issue. Bulls president Michael Reinsdorf <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/10/02/united-center-1901-project-transformation-break-ground-next-summer-wirtz-reinsdorf" >said</a> in 2024 that United Center lots typically maxed out around 75% occupancy. City-dwelling fans utilizing public transportation contributes to that.</p><p>The capacity of higher-demand lots, however, can be an issue. And then there's the matter of drive-up parking prices, which have risen by as much as $15-30 at some lots.</p><p>It's now much cheaper to purchase parking coupons online in advance (for as little as $20). Many fans don't know that, though, and have experienced some sticker shock from their car windows. It's also worth noting advance coupons aren't publicly available for some closer-in lots.</p><p>The arena spokesperson said parking prices are impacted by operating expenses and a 35.25% tax rate paid to the city, county and state.</p>

entries.title: White Sox assistant general manager Josh Barfield is a candidate for Astros' open GM job: report
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> surprising 2026 success has brought a lot of things the franchise hasn’t seen in a while — multiple All-Star representatives, home playoff games at Rate Field, and the potential for front office brain drain.</p><p>Most recently, The Athletic reported that Sox assistant general manager Josh Barfield is a candidate for the Astros’ general manager position, which has been open since the American League West champions fired Dana Brown in August. Hired away from his role as the Diamondbacks director of player development in September of 2023, Barfield recently completed his third full season as a White Sox assistant GM. Near the very end of it, before the White Sox swept their way through the wild-card round in two games, Barfield was seen on the field at Daikin Park in Houston having a lengthy chat with Astros owner Jim Crane.</p><p>Owning significant prior history with the current White Sox directors of both player development (Paul Janish) and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/07/white-sox-nearing-surprising-al-central-title-behind-remodeled-player-acquisition-process-chris-getz-josh-barfield-david-keller-miguel-vargas-tristan-peters-luis-castillo-curtis-mead-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" ><u>the recently overhauled department of acquisitions</u></a> (Matt Grabowski), Barfield has had a weighty influence in the team’s recent course changes in both areas. With the White Sox having improved their major-league results by 19 wins in 2025 before their 23-win jump in 2026, Barfield was considered for potential promotions by other clubs last offseason as well.</p><p>“It’s the best decision I could have ever made,” Barfield said this spring of joining the White Sox. “Because I really believe in what we’re doing.”</p><p>The Sox are already trying to fill one gap in their front office mix this winter, in the wake of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/12/white-sox-amateur-scouting-director-mike-shirley-resigns-chris-getz-garrett-crochet-colson-montgomery-grant-taylor-jacob-gonzalez-hagen-smith-caleb-bonemer" >amateur scouting director Mike Shirley resigning in September,</a> which sources said stemmed from an internal investigation into his conduct. In his media availability last week, White Sox general manager Chris Getz said the team intends to make a hire under the title “director of amateur acquisitions.”</p><p>League sources have indicated the White Sox have been interviewing candidates for the role. While Getz’s major hires have leaned toward bringing in new voices from other organizations, and he said in September that the Sox were “looking into a different way of doing business on that front” in regards to amateur scouting, internal candidates — including at the scouting supervisor level — have been interviewed as well.</p>

entries.title: Polish poet turns words of Holocaust victims, perpetrators into shards of 'memory activism'
entries.summary: <p><i>    during the war we laid out bodies like wood</i><br><i>    but after the war we laid out wood in the forest  </i><br><i>    like bodies freshly felled.</i></p><p>Grzegorz Kwiatkowski is not Jewish, but reads his poetry like an Orthodox Jew praying, bending at the waist, rocking forward and back.</p><p><i>    I went with my child to the forest and cried helplessly with him</i><br><i>    tears dripped from my eyes and the child wiped them away with his hand</i><br><i>    and I so regretted I had brought him into the world</i></p><p>He's in a third floor conference room at the University of Chicago, reading to about two dozen people, gathered on Monday morning to hear him.</p><p><i>     they didn't know where to run since it was an open field and they ran in circles</i><br><i>     how we laughed</i><br><i>     and before we killed them</i><br><i>     we even whistled some tunes</i></p><p>Kwiatkowski is reading — loudly, with little inflection — from his book <a class="Link" href="https://raintaxi.com/crops/" target="_blank" >“Crops,”</a> translated from Polish by Peter Constantine. More a pamphlet than a book: 19 small, hard, stone-like poems over 32 pages.</p><p><i>     my father</i><br><i>     a decent office worker in the railways</i><br><i>     never took part in any of the shootings</i><br><i>     he was just doing his job</i><br><i>     organizing transports</i><br><i>     eastward and westward</i><br><i>     north and south</i><br><i>     back and forth</i></p><p>The poems are his, but the words aren't — he gathered them from taped testimonies, combining victims, perpetrators and bystanders. </p><p>"I didn't change any of the words," he says. "But still I'm framing it. I'm choosing the fragments. I'm responsible."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-510000" name="module-510000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>I'm here because he sent me "Crops." I read it in less than 10 minutes, but the book rearranged my brain, providing necessary starkness, a counterpoint that I've been missing. Over the years, we've seen the Holocaust transformed into entertainment, especially on social media. Once there was one Anne Frank. Now there are 6 million. The Holocaust has been retrofitted into a bracing tale of courage, resistance, and redemption. The Holocaust is not a tale of courage, resistance and redemption. It is an epic of cruelty, obedience and horror.</p><p>Kwiatkowski agrees.</p><p>"Most art about the Holocaust is kitsch," he says.</p><p>Kwiatkowski gathers words, but doesn't mince them, which makes him a controversial figure in Poland, where depictions of the Holocaust that don't relentlessly depict the Poles as either victims or heroes are highly unwelcome. The Polish government once demanded that the Sun-Times take down a column of mine suggesting otherwise and, when the paper refused, we were sued. We won, because this is America. Whether it stays America...</p><p><i>I was refused because according to them one couldn't write about the occupation this way</i><br><i>they said I was opening the window so narrowly</i><br><i>just a sliver could be seen</i><br><i>that I look at the Holocaust with just one eye</i><br><i>and speak it in a whisper</i></p><p><i>one must write differently about the Holocaust</i><br><i>the window must be thrown wide open and one must shout</i><br><i>not whisper the way I do</i></p><p>Kwiatkowski's poems are shouts; I reproduced only the milder ones, in consideration of sensitive readers. Nobody's head is sawed off here. </p><p>He is from Gdansk, where he founded a rock group, Trupa Trupa. He is currently artist-in-residence at Yale University's Fortunoff Video Archive for Holocaust Testimonies.</p><p>When Kwiatkowski was 9, his grandfather, who had been a prisoner in the Stuthoff concentration camp, returned to the camp for the first time, taking him along, an experience that transformed him.</p><p>"I didn't know what was going on. Later, I felt he gave me one of the most important lessons in my life," said Kwiatkowski. "A very dark one, but I started to ask myself questions: why people are building gas chambers? Why people are building concentration camps? And they're doing it on and on and on. It's a never-ending story, unfortunately."</p><p>We call them "detention facilities" now, and while ICE isn't killing people en masse, the truth is, we don't know what's going on inside those remote facilities, and many Americans don't want to know. If you haven't noticed, we live in a country where ethnic groups are routinely demonized — Somalis in Minnesota, immigrants everywhere — and masked government thugs pull people off the street for no reason at all. The bedrock of any Holocaust.</p><p>Kwiatkowski calls what he does "memory activism," the poems, "the main point of my life."</p><p>Along with his wife and children. Kwiatkowski mentions that his wife, who is Jewish — he didn't know that when they married, he said, calling it her “family secret” — put up a mezuzah on the <i>inside</i> of the front door frame of their apartment. So the neighbors wouldn't see. Because you know how neighbors can be.</p><p><i>most of the townsfolk came to see their murdered neighbors</i><br><i>some lay still alive in the pits</i><br><i>Good morning Mr. Brumberg</i><br><i>Good morning Mrs. Bulkin</i><br><i>Good morning</i><br><i>Good morning</i><br></p>
